#803. Where does Kane rank among all-time England greats?

Harry Kane is now England's most-capped men's player as well as his country's record goalscorer, but harder to quantify is where these achievements place him among the Three Lions' greatest ever players.

This is a tricky debate with so many variables and a timescale as old as the game itself and, to my mind, not merely a determination of a player's individual ability but also a measure of their impact upon the nation's psyche.

Ballon d'Or winners Stanley Matthews, Kevin Keegan and Michael Owen would surely have a shout if the criteria was such, not to mention genius technicians such as Glenn Hoddle, Chris Waddle and John Barnes.

Likewise, if any England boss managed to extract the best from Paul Scholes, Steven Gerrard and Frank Lampard they would be surely making a classic late dart from midfield.

But to qualify as one of the greatest England players of all time, you need the above ability combined with an impactful overall contribution - those memorable moments and an element of longevity - in a Three Lions shirt.

It might be controversial then to leave out Geoff Hurst, who produced the most recognisable performance in England history, while the man he replaced, Jimmy Greaves, would be a shoo-in were it not for injury earlier in the tournament.

It is also hard to rank the contribution of those whose best football came outside of major tournaments and before the dawn of continental competitions - see Eddie Hapgood, Tom Finney, Nat Lofthouse, Dixie Dean et al.

There are only 10 spots, after all, so here we go.

Spice Boy. Celebrity. Galactico. There is no argument David Beckham is one of the most iconic England players of all time, but he backed it up on the pitch, too.

Beckham was the face of the Three Lions for a generation, and to his credit managed to overcome the vicious fallout of his red card against Argentina in 1998.

At times he seemed to single-handedly carry England, most notably scoring a 93rd-minute free-kick against Greece to qualify for the 2002 World Cup.

Beckham's former team-mate Gary Neville called him the "most influential player out of England in transforming football".

It's true. On top of 115 caps, Beckham was part of Manchester United's 1999 Treble-winning outfit - finishing Ballon d'Or runner-up - before joining Real Madrid.

His profile was truly global with spells at LA Galaxy, AC Milan and Paris St-Germain.

David Beckham scored 17 goals for England, including five free-kicks

There's arguably no England star fans forged an emotional attachment with more than Gazza - crying with him in 1990, rejoicing in his spectacular effort against Scotland and desperately willing him to connect during that Euro 96 semi-final defeat by Germany.

Gascoigne won 57 caps and scored 10 goals. At his peak, he was captivating - transcending football as a cultural phenomenon during the summers of '90 and '96, having joined a star-studded Serie A between those tournaments.

Creative, unpredictable, vulnerable. He was a loveable but flawed genius.

He suffered long-term injuries as England missed out on Euro 92 and the World Cup in the USA, but helped the Three Lions qualify for France 98 before being dropped from the final squad, famously wrecking boss Glenn Hoddle's office.

Gascoigne, Poborsky , McCoist - Goals that defined Euro 96

Goalscorers often grab the headlines but I've tried to credit players across positions and eras. From a defensive point of view Ashley Cole, arguably England's best-ever full-back, was close to making it.

But instead it's the great Billy Wright, the first men's player to surpass a century of international caps, including a remarkable 70 successive appearances over eight years.

Wright captained his country on 90 occasions, a joint-record recently broken by Kane, taking in three World Cups with impressive longevity for his era.

He was a true one-club man, winning three league titles, the FA Cup and becoming unofficial "world champions" with Wolves in 1954 - helping inspire the birth of the European Cup - while finishing Ballon d'Or runner-up to Alfredo di Stefano in 1957.

Billy Wright captained England 90 times - a record shared with Bobby Moore until Harry Kane recently surpassed the pair

It feels a little premature to include a 23-year-old with the bulk of his England career ahead of him, but that shows the impact Jude Bellingham has already made for England and Real Madrid.

A Champions League winner, the midfielder has also appeared at four major tournaments for the Three Lions, becoming the youngest player to do so at the delayed Euro 2020, aged 17.

But his role in helping carry England to the final two years ago and a third-place finish at last summer's World Cup really make him stand out.

Bellingham has delivered those moments a nation collectively remembers. The last-gasp overhead kick against Slovakia in 2024, a quickfire double at the Azteca against Mexico this summer and 93rd-minute quarter-final winner against Norway.

His seven goals at this World Cup were more than any previous Three Lions player in a single edition, the solo effort against France a thing of beauty.

The former Birmingham and Dortmund man doesn't turn 24 until June but has already collected 61 England caps and netted 14 times. As Roy Keane put it, Bellingham has the potential to be one of the "greatest of all time".

Ten of Bellingham's 14 England goals have come at major tournaments

In terms of natural ability, Wayne Rooney is among England's greatest ever talents.

Bursting on to the scene at Euro 2004 as an electric 18-year-old, having become England's youngest player and scorer the previous year, convinced fans and media the teen sensation could carry the Three Lions to glory in Portugal.

He bounced World Cup winner Lilian Thuram around in England's opener against France in a glimpse of his precocious strength, before scoring twice against both Switzerland and Croatia.

Who knows how far England would have gone had Rooney not been injured against Portugal in the quarter-final?

He was unable to replicate the impact of his first Euros - a red card at World Cup 2006, suspension for the Euro 2012 group stage, seven goals across six major tournaments - but was an all-rounder who brought more than just goals.

Rooney also won it all with Manchester United, becoming the club's all-time top scorer, and finished his 15-year England career with 53 goals from 120 caps.

Rooney burst on to the scene as an 18-year-old at Euro 2004

There has to be a place for a goalkeeper, and Gordon Banks is the safest pair of hands.

A World Cup winner in 1966, his save from Pele four years later against Brazil is one of the most iconic of all time. Pele called him a "goalkeeper with magic".

Banks spent the majority of his career at Leicester and Stoke, winning a League Cup with each, and earned 73 England caps overall between 1963 and 1972.

His incredible athleticism and reflexes saw the shot-stopper named Fifa's best goalkeeper for five successive years between 1966 and 1971.

Banks and Pele became good friends following the goalkeeper's iconic save in 1970

Gary Lineker's early club career did not deliver the silverware as his goals deserved, netting 40 times but finishing league and FA Cup runner-up in his one season at Everton before joining Barcelona.

He scored a Clasico hat-trick and won the Copa del Rey and Cup Winner's Cup, however, before adding an FA Cup with Tottenham in 1991.

Lineker netted 283 club goals (and famously no cards) in total across spells with Leicester, Everton, Barcelona, Spurs and Nagoya Grampus Eight.

But as a player Lineker is most renowned for his contribution in an England shirt, winning the Golden Boot as they reached the World Cup quarter-finals in 1986 - finishing Ballon d'Or runner-up that year - before netting another four as the Three Lions reached the semi-finals in 1990.

Lineker equalised against West Germany before England crashed out on penalties.

However, having missed a spot-kick against Brazil, he finished one short of Bobby Charlton's elusive goal record when his international career ended after Euro 92.

Gary Lineker scored 48 goals in 80 games for England

Harry Kane is undoubtedly England's most important and influential player of a generation - it is hard to imagine how this Three Lions side functions once the skipper hangs up his boots.

The Bayern Munich striker, complete with Ballon d'Or, has been scoring goals for his country for almost 12 years, the first just 79 seconds into his debut after coming off the bench against Lithuania in March 2015.

Rooney's goalscoring benchmark is long in his rear view mirror - you wouldn't bank against Kane doubling his nearest rival's figure once his England days are over.

They have come on the biggest stage, too - 21 in 36 appearances from three World Cups and European Championships apiece, winning the World Cup Golden Boot in 2018.

Kane has come closer to winning a major tournament than any England men's captain since Bobby Moore - losing two World Cup semi-finals and back-to-back Euros finals. Team-mate Bellingham called him the "greatest player that has ever played for England".

"I think we'll appreciate him even more in another 10, 15, 20 years when you look back and see what he has achieved," said ex-England goalkeeper Paul Robinson.

In many ways, Bobby Moore would be the complete modern-day defender. Cool as you like under pressure, elegant in possession, a great passing range off both feet and, as his West Ham and England team-mate Geoff Hurst said: "Nobody out-ran him and nobody out-jumped him."

Moore's positioning and timing was perfect, that iconic tackle on Jairzinho at the 1970 World Cup the finest example of his poise and precision when defending.

He was also a composed and influential leader. A player built for the big occasions. England boss Sir Alf Ramsey called him: "My lieutenant on the field, a cool, calculated footballer I could trust with my life."

The Barking-born centre-back won the FA Cup and European Cup Winners' Cup with West Ham but his finest moment was leading England to glory in 1966. He was only 25 at the time, having become his country's youngest captain three years earlier.

In 1970, after the Bogota bracelet incident, Moore was imperious as England reached the quarter-finals before bowing out to West Germany.

It was, however, the final group game against Brazil, the most exciting side on the planet, that produced some of the most recognisable and renowned images in sporting history - not only Moore's tackle and Banks' save but the defender swapping shirts with Pele after the final whistle.

"The greatest defender I ever played against," was the Brazilian's verdict.

Bobby Moore is the only man to captain the Three Lions to World Cup glory

For more than a generation, Sir Bobby's England goalscoring record remained unmatched. It took 55 years from his 49th and final strike against Colombia in 1970 until Rooney surpassed him with his half century in 2015.

Charlton was, as Alan Shearer put it, "not only a great goalscorer but a scorer of great goals" and played a pivotal part of the Three Lions' World Cup success in 1966, netting three times on the way to the final.

A scampering run from the halfway line followed by a trademark long-range strike into the corner at Wembley gave England's campaign lift-off against Mexico, before he scored twice against Eusebio's Portugal in the semi-finals.

Manager Ramsey called the buccaneering midfielder his "lynchpin" as England triumphed over West Germany in the showpiece and those performances helped Charlton win the Ballon d'Or later that year.

He'd be runner-up in successive years after that, too.

Charlton won 106 England caps and was a star for Manchester United, with Rooney also the one to pip his club-record 249 goals for the Old Trafford outfit.

A survivor of the Munich air disaster on 6 February 1958, which killed 23 people including eight players and three members of the club's staff, Charlton won three league titles, an FA Cup and most poignantly the European Cup in 1968.

"England's greatest ever player," Lineker previously told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"He was unique. Wherever you go in the world, even if they didn't speak the language, they knew two words - Bobby Charlton."

Charlton's England goal record stood for more than half a century

#801. Travis Barker Reveals Precancer Diagnosis Led Him to Quit Smoking Weed

Travis Barker said being diagnosed with "precancer of the esophagus" led him to stop smoking weed: "I thought I could be like Willie Nelson and smoke to the day I die."

Travis Barker's health scare has led him to dump weed.

The Blink-182 drummer said he stopped smoking marijuana after receiving a troubling diagnosis.

"I only quit because I got diagnosed with precancer of the esophagus," Barker shared on the Nov. 11 episode of the Big Bro with Kid Cudi podcast. "I loved blunts and I would smoke too much."

In fact, the 50-year-old—who shares 3-year-old son Rocky Barker with wife Kourtney Kardashian, as well as kids Alabama Barker, 20, Landon Barker, 23, and stepdaughter Atiana de la Hoya , 27, with ex Shanna Moakler—said he "would have never stopped" until his doctor told him that it was a "serious" case.

Still, the "Dumpweed" rocker thinks about lighting up "all the time."

"I miss it," he admitted. "I'm not gonna lie."

However, Barker has since channeled that craving into a healthier habit: running.

"I've found even however many years later now, 20 years later, couple miles a day keeps the demons away," he continued. "My running started getting bigger and more important to me than smoking."

The "All the Small Things" musician noted that jogging—which he took up following his 2008 near-fatal plane crash—also played a large part in helping him overcome his addiction to prescription painkillers and opioids.

"It really helped me stay sober 'cause you can't run you a half a marathon if you're doing drugs," Barker explained. "It's going to be the hardest 13.1 miles of your life."

He added, "It's good, man. It's like therapy."

CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. — NASA has officially launched the Moon Base Student Challenge, asking students to help build humanity's future on the moon. And there's $1 million in prizes up for grabs for the winners.

To build and sustain a base on the moon, NASA will have to solve a myriad of problems. And they're looking to the next generation for help, the space agency's chief Jared Isaacman said Sunday (Nov. 8).

"We are inviting students from across the country to help solve some of the problems that stand between humanity and a permanent presence on another world," Isaacman said. "We're putting 1 million in prizes together to support the best ideas and recognize the teams behind them."

Isaacman made this announcement wearing his blue flight suit from the rocket garden at NASA's Kennedy Space Center Visitor Center amidst the agency's MAX POWER air show event. Just the day before, he flew fighter jets in that suit and even jumped out of a plane, skydiving into the event. Soon after this announcement, he was flying another fighter plane above the crowd.

The audience for this announcement was filled with students of all ages. Some young children wearing costume spacesuits squeezed as close as they could to the front of the room while teenagers considering their futures listened intently. It was clear that Isaacman's presence and words were landing with this group.

But what moon base challenges does NASA want to see these students tackle? In short, all of them.

"The moon base will allow us to conduct groundbreaking science, test new technologies, and prepare again for where we inevitably go next, which is the red planet," he said. "But before any of that can happen, we have an awful lot of problems that need to be solved."

"We need ways to generate power through the long lunar night. We need to protect our astronauts from that incredibly harsh and dangerous and demanding environment on the surface. We need to move people and equipment around on the surface and support human life three days away from Earth," Isaacman said, illustrating just a few of the big issues that present with the concept of a moon base.

This challenge is open to high school and post-secondary students based in the U.S. For participating students, they will form teams that will work on an idea from one of six different technical topics related to creating and running a moon base. These six topics include power systems, habitats, communications, mobility, life support and astronaut safety.

This will be what Isaacman described as a "multi-phase competition that mirrors how ideas are developed actually in the aerospace industry."

"Teams will first submit concepts, then they're going to refine them, and finalists will have the opportunity to present their solutions directly to NASA leaders and stakeholders," he further explained.

"The prize money is great for sure, but the the real opportunity is to work on problems NASA is actively trying to solve right now, so students don't need to wait to graduation to contribute to that effort," Isaacman added.

Right now, NASA has a long road ahead of them before a moon base is actually built. In mid-2027, the agency is planning to launch its Artemis III mission which will see a crew of four astronauts practice rendezvous maneuvers with two different lunar landers. If all goes to plan, this will be followed by Artemis IV landing humans on the moon's surface for the first time since the final Apollo mission in 1972.

The agency is making these big steps forward to not just a crewed return to the moon, but a sustained, long-term return to the moon. However, knowing that a fully-fledged moon base is still firmly in the future, they are banking on the ingenuity, creativity and passion of

If you're a student or know a student interested in participating in this challenge, you can find more information on NASA's website here. Interested students can register until Jan. 25, 2027.

#799. Permanent daylight saving time has a dark side, scientists warn

Keeping daylight saving time in effect all year could bring brighter evenings, but new research suggests the change would come with a troubling consequence for American children. A nationwide switch could result in at least 2 billion additional trips to school in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks while reducing children's exposure to important morning sunlight.

The debate over permanent daylight saving time has gained momentum in Washington, D.C. This past summer, the U.S. House of Representatives approved legislation that would eliminate the annual return to standard time in the fall. Nineteen states, including Washington, have already approved measures supporting the change, which would take effect in those states if the federal bill becomes law.

The legislation remains stalled in the Senate, with school start times emerging as a major concern. Permanent daylight saving time (DST) would push sunrise an hour later during the winter months, leaving mornings darker from November through March. Although this would affect everyone traveling early in the day, researchers at the University of Washington wanted to understand what it would mean specifically for children heading to school.

Permanent Daylight Saving Time Could Add Billions of Dark School Commutes

To measure the potential impact, the research team examined 14 of the 19 states that have already approved permanent daylight saving time measures. They combined school enrollment figures, individual school start times, and geographic coordinates to determine how frequently students would need to travel to school before sunrise. The researchers then calculated the total number of these trips under the proposed system and compared it with the current practice of changing clocks twice a year.

The results revealed substantial increases. In Washington state alone, permanent daylight saving time would produce nearly 35 million additional school commutes in darkness. Similar patterns emerged across the other 13 states, with Georgia showing the largest increase at approximately 71 million additional dark trips.

When the researchers extended their findings to estimate the nationwide impact, they calculated that permanent daylight saving time would create at least 2 billion more trips to school before sunrise compared with the current system.

The potential consequences go beyond inconvenient mornings. An analysis of U.S. traffic collision records found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely to occur during dark mornings as after sunrise. The findings were published October 29 in the journal Current Biology.

"It's called the 'Sunshine Protection Act' because you get an extra hour of light at the end of the day. But you will take that hour from the morning. You could call it the Sunshine Destruction Act," said senior author Horacio de la Iglesia, a professor of biology at the University of Washington. "These dark mornings will inequitably affect children who have to go to school at a certain time. It's a very tangible metric that anybody from any state or socioeconomic background can relate to. Nobody wants their kids to go to school in the dark."

Why Morning Sunlight Matters for Children's Health

Beyond concerns about traffic safety, losing access to morning sunlight could interfere with the body's natural daily rhythms. Bright light early in the day helps synchronize the circadian clock, the internal timing system that influences sleep, mood, appetite, and other important functions. When people receive too little morning light, maintaining these biological rhythms can become more difficult.

For children, who must typically follow fixed school schedules, darker mornings could mean missing a valuable opportunity to receive daylight at a time when their bodies need it.

"When we send kids to school in the dark, we are depriving them from an opportunity to get that morning daylight," said lead author Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, a postdoctoral researcher in biology at the University of Washington. "We were asking what's the cost for these children. We wanted actual numbers, a real number of kids based on the geographic location of each school."

The researchers also identified which communities would experience the greatest changes. Schools located near the western boundaries of time zones, including those in Forks, Washington, would be particularly affected because sunrise already occurs relatively late in those locations. Districts that begin classes early in the morning would face similarly large increases in dark commutes.

Mississippi and Alabama offer striking examples. Schools in both states begin, on average, before 8 a.m. Under the current clock system, each state has approximately 2 million school trips in darkness. With permanent daylight saving time, that figure would rise to more than 20 million trips per state.

"Some districts probably never experience a dark commute under the current system, and, if this passes, suddenly they will wake up to this new reality that their kids are going to school in the dark," Rodríguez Ferrante said. "Keep in mind that we used the actual start time listed for each school, and a lot of schools offer breakfast or other things before school, so the kids could be getting there even earlier."

Why the 2 Billion Estimate May Be Too Low

Although the researchers used detailed school information to calculate changes in 14 states, their nationwide estimate required broader assumptions. To project what would happen if the entire United States adopted permanent daylight saving time, they assumed students would generally be leaving for school at around 8 a.m.

Because many children begin traveling earlier, the team believes the projected increase of approximately 2 billion dark commutes may substantially underestimate the actual impact.

"For the estimation, we assumed students would be leaving home around 8 a.m.," Rodríguez Ferrante said. "That's pretty late, so our calculation is likely an underestimation of the real number."

The findings also raise questions about efforts to improve teenagers' sleep by delaying high school start times. Adolescents typically have biological clocks that shift later than those of younger children and adults, making later school schedules beneficial. The researchers argue that permanently moving clocks forward could undermine some of those gains by making morning sunlight less accessible.

One possible solution would be to start school later to compensate for the darker mornings. However, de la Iglesia argues that such a change could have ripple effects throughout daily life, potentially requiring families and workplaces to adjust their schedules as well.

"I've heard the argument, 'If we're in permanent DST, we can just delay the school start time to address these issues,'" de la Iglesia said. "Well, if we do that, you will end up going to work later. And everything is going to get delayed. You will get out of work an hour later, and you will miss the opportunity to enjoy your evening light. And essentially, we're just going to be realigning everybody to solar time. That, by definition, is Standard Time."

The researchers' findings highlight a central tradeoff in the debate over permanent daylight saving time. While eliminating seasonal clock changes would provide more evening sunlight during winter, the additional daylight would come at the expense of morning light, potentially affecting children's safety, sleep, and daily routines.

Additional study authors include high school student Daniel Zhang and University of Washington biology undergraduates Nirekh Dasika, Alicia Nam, Jessie Lu, Navneet Tumber, Elena Kully-Rivera, Viridian Klei, and Micaela E. Romero.

#798. Julianne Hough Reacts to Derek Hough’s Sister-to-Lover Moment on DWTS

After Derek Hough reacted to fellow Dancing With the Stars judge Carrie Ann Inaba’s viral sister-to-lover comment on the show, his sister Julianne Hough shared her response.

An awkward moment on Dancing With the Stars basically left Julianne Hough thinking, “Oh, brother.”

The DWTS co-host reacted to a cringey moment from the Nov. 10 episode when her brother—and judge on the competition series—Derek Hough made a quip about sibling dynamics.

ICYMI, after Paralympian Ezra Frech and his pro partner Daniella Karagach, who have detailed their sibling-like relationship this season, performed a sensual Argentine tango, they received some shocking praise from judge Carrie Ann Inaba.

“You were able to stay so centered on yourself while also delivering the story that I want so much with this dance,” she said. “The intimacy, turning your sister into your lover for one night is all good.”

As Ezra and Daniella were left in surprise, co-host Alfonso Ribeiro said, “Sister lover, that’s awkward.” And as the mic was turned over to Derek, he quipped with laughter, “Tell me about it. That was weird.”

The moment prompted a flurry of comments online, as fans pointed out how Julianne and Derek have been paired up for some sensual dances over the years. As one fan wrote on Threads, “Derek adding in ‘tell me about it’ after Carrie Ann gave Ezra and Daniella credit for doing an intimate dance when they feel like siblings had me GIGGGGGGGLING.”

After all, the 38-year-old only added a shrugging emoji while sharing a Thread post to her Instagram Stories Nov. 12 that read, “Derek adding in ‘tell me about it’ after Carrie Ann gave Ezra and Daniella credit for doing an intimate dance when they feel like siblings had me GIGGGGGGGLING.”

But Julianne appeared to sidestep the awkwardness with one smooth move. After all, the 38-year-old re-posted the comment on her Instagram Story and simply added a shrugging emoji to prove her nonchalance.

But while Julianne may have shimmied away from this week’s snafu, it’s not the first sibling-centric shuffle that Carrie Ann has caused between her and Derek. In fact, after Carrie Ann paired them up in 2014 for an intimate routine, fans thought the Houghs were married.

“Our first thing that we ever did on Dancing with the Stars was the live tour,” Julianne said on a September 2025 episode of the Chicks in the Office podcast. “Carrie Ann was the one who choreographed everything, and she got us to do a rumba together. You guys, that’s the dance of love that my brother and I had to dance together.”

“Our names in the program were ‘Derek and Julianne Hough,’ so everybody thought we were married and were doing this rumba,” Julianne continued. “When people found out we were brother and sister? I remember there was one venue, and we just heard, ‘That’s just wrong!’”

For a deeper dive into the siblings’—yes, siblings’—family tree, keep reading…

The Hough family patriarch is originally from Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, and met future wife Mariann Heaton on the ballroom team at Ricks College (now Brigham Young University-Idaho).

Bruce and Mariann—both from Mormon families and the children of ballroom-dancing parents—settled in Salt Lake City. There he worked as a communications executive and co-founded supplement maker Nutraceutical Corporation, which, according to Deseret News, reached a valuation of $300 million under his watch before it was sold in 2017.

Bruce also ventured into politics, serving two terms as state Republican Party chair and running for congress in 2023.

While he didn't win that race, he told Deseret News at the time that he was running for his family's future. "I’ve got 10 kids, I’ve got 22 grandkids and growing," he explained. "And I really feel that America’s promise is in jeopardy for those grandkids especially."

Of his most famous offspring, he quipped, "I never thought that those dance lessons would pay off,” noting that he took the most pride in hearing from others that son Derek Hough and daughter Julianne Hough were some of the "kindest people…in the entertainment business.”

In addition to Derek and Julianne, Bruce shares daughters Sharee Hough Selman, Marabeth Poole and Katherine Hough with Mariann. After they divorced in the late 1990s, he married Debra Francom Hough, also a parent of five.

Mariann grew up in Idaho Falls with three brothers.

She and Bruce were in the process of divorcing when Julianne and Derek, then 10 and 13, moved to London to attend the Italia Conti Academy of Theatre Arts.

Their leaving was "devastating," Mariann recalled on a 2019 episode of The Minds Gym podcast. But they wanted to dance and, she explained, "The biggest thing that kept me going is that I grew up feeling very dominated over and controlled. Love my parents, but that was like a generational thing."

However, she added, "I'm grateful for that now because…it made me sway to I love having free agency." It was also "so important" for her to pass that on to her kids, she said, and "all of them are so not afraid to go travel and do all these things."

Mariann, now based in Franklin, Tenn., is a painter and has credited husband Aaron Nelson for supporting and encouraging her work as an artist.

Sharee married husband Mark Selman when she was 19 and they share six kids.

The eldest of Bruce and Mariann's brood danced at Ballet West in Utah and these days runs her own fitness business, Hough Werks, teaching yoga and dance.

Her "dynamic" firstborn "just came into this world with a lot of energy," Mariann said on The Minds Gym. Sharee's "little mind was just going all the time, just super creative" and "self-motivated."

Moreover, with 11 years between Sharee and her youngest sister, "Julianne thinks she has two moms."

Marabeth is "just a beautiful spirit" who "loves her own space," Mariann said of her second child, and she "puts on these little retreats in Nashville for women."

She left Utah for Music City to "be a country star," baby sister Julianne shared on the Not Skinny but Not Fat podcast in September 2025, and now makes the most of her positive energy as a realtor and holistic health coach, as well as a singer-songwriter.

Marabeth married Michael Poole in 2002 and they live in Nashville with son Aidan.

Daughter Katherine, a mother of three, "just makes you smile," Mariann said on The Minds Gym, "and she's just real."

The esthetician was in a relationship with Tony Schnur before his death from brain cancer in 2023. "It’s unfair that I found my soulmate, my best friend, my partner in life, only to lose you too soon," Katherine posted on Instragram in February 2025, marking the second anniversary of his passing. "I miss you every day."

But Katherine has persevered, Julianne gushing on Not Skinny But Not Fat, "She has three beautiful daughters and she has all these activities and she plans all these things, and I'm in awe of her."

And on Sept. 24, 2025, Katherine shared that she had found love again, writing on Instagram alongside a montage of sweet photos, "After walking through so much loss and heartache, I never imagined I’d find this kind of love again. Chris is the man I prayed for, kind, generous, loving, patient, and such a gift not only to me but to my girls."

Born May 17, 1985, Derek joined Dancing With the Stars as a pro in 2007. He won the Mirrorball Trophy a record six times and is a four-time Emmy winner for choreography.

After his last competitive turn around the floor in 2016, Derek returned to DWTS as a fulltime judge in 2020.

He met fellow dancer Hayley Erbert in 2015 and, after navigating some "insane obstacles," as he put it on Couple Things With Shawn Johnson and Andrew East, they got married in August 2023.

As a couple they powered through Hayley's life-threatening health scare, a brain hemorrhage that required emergency surgery just four months after their wedding, and in July 2025 they announced they were expecting their first child together.

Posting a photo of dad Bruce dancing at his and Hayley's wedding, Derek wrote on Facebook in April 2024, "Smart, kind and thoughtful. I hope to be as good as a father as he has been to his family."

The baby of the Hough family was born July 20,1988. She joined DWTS in 2007 along with Derek and proceeded to win her first two seasons on the show.

She left in 2009 to pursue acting and scored a breakthrough role in 2010's Burlesque (though her big-screen debut was actually playing an unnamed Hogwarts student in 2001's Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone) before scoring the lead in the 2011 Footloose remake. Julianne returned to the ballroom as a judge from 2014 to 2017, winning an Emmy for choreography along the way, and has cohosted DWTS with Alfonso Ribeiro since 2023.

Julianne married Brooks Laich in 2017 but they split up in 2020, eventually finalizing their divorce in 2022.

She said on The Jamie Kern Lima Show in 2024 that going through a divorce gave her a chance to "reconnect" with her mom and dad, and they "showed up" for her.

"I needed that," Julianne explained. "I reclaimed my parental relationship with them and I got to be the kid and they got to take care of me. And that was the most healing [thing]."

Reflecting on her and Derek becoming the stars of the family, Julianne said on Not Skinny But Not Fat that there was "no jealousy" between their other siblings, "but there is a sadness that maybe there wasn't an opportunity for them to experience it."

Sharee, Marabeth and Katherine are "so, so, so happy," Julianne continued. "They have great lives, and they love their life. But we had an opportunity that they didn't have, and it's hard.”

And while she and Derek have a special connection, "they were super close as sisters growing up,” Julianne said. “So, I didn't get to have the closeness of sisters and that bond. [And] they have marriages and kids and I don't have that experience."

Meanwhile, all five siblings "get along really well," Mariann said on The Minds Gym. "I think the hard part is being away from each other, because there is some kind of a synergy when they all get together."

Sienna Spiro won’t be making the trip to Australia next week, as planned, where she was expected to perform at the 2026 ARIA Awards.

The rising British singer and songwriter pulls out of the 40th annual awards ceremony, due to the physical demands of her latest tour.

“I am so incredibly sorry I won’t be able to make it to the ARIA Awards this year,” she writes in a post, shared on ARIA’s Instagram Stories. “I’ve been looking forward to coming back for months, however this tour has taken its toll on me and my voice.”

Spiro recently completed the North American run of the My House World Tour, in support of her hit debut album, Visitor. Explore Blusher Sienna Spiro See latest videos, charts and news

Music Video AI Deepfake: 'Jensen Don't Sweat It'

Spiro was the first international performer announced for this year’s ARIAs, to be presented Wednesday, Nov. 18 at Sydney’s Hordern Pavilion. Her trip to the ARIAs was meant to be Spiro’s second trip to Australia following an intimate fan event last year at Pleasure Club in Newtown, Sydney. She’ll return in January 2027 for her eight-date My House Tour of Australia and New Zealand, which includes two nights at the Hordern. “I am incredibly grateful to the ARIA team for the opportunity and so sad to let you all down,” she writes.

At just 21 years of age, the Londoner has already accumulated more than 36 million monthly listeners on Spotify, headline sponsor of the ARIAs, and upwards of 2 billion total streams; bagged three simultaneous Billboard Hot 100 singles; and six entries on the ARIA Singles Chart. “Die On This Hill” is certified platinum by ARIA, while “You Stole The Show,” “MAYBE,” “Material Lover” and “The Visitor” are all certified Gold in these parts.

In her place, Atlantic Records-signed, Melbourne-based hyperpop trio Blusher will join the line up for the ARIAs, reads a statement from the trade body, for what will “be an unforgettable night honoring four decades of Australian music.”

With eight nominations each, Tame Impala and Genesis Owusu lead the pack for the 40th annual ARIA Awards, while Ecca Vandal, winner of the 2026 Australian Music Prize, is close behind with seven nods.

The 2026 ARIA Awards is supported by Destination NSW, in partnership with Spotify, and will be live on Paramount+ and broadcast on 10. Performances and moments will also be available on the @ARIA.official YouTube channel.

Starfish Space's first Otter has died, just a month after it reached the final frontier.

The Seattle startup announced on Tuesday (Nov. 3) that its Otter 24C satellite suffered a glitch in low Earth orbit (LEO) and is not recoverable.

The anomaly killed an ambitious mission in the cradle, as Otter 24C was still in the commissioning phase.

Otter 24C launched Oct. 1 on SpaceX's Transporter-18 mission, a rideshare flight that carried a total of 130 payloads to LEO (including a prototype satellite for Project Suncatcher, Google's planned AI constellation).

The Starfish satellite was flying a mission for NASA called Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability, or SSPICY for short. The goal was to "demonstrate technologies necessary for future debris-removal missions as well as for future applications in the servicing and inspection of active spacecraft," according to NASA's SSPICY site.

"This advances NASA's in-space manufacturing and assembly (ISAM) goals to ensure a sustainable space operating environment and builds towards a future where objects can be assembled, repaired and maintained in space, significantly expanding possibilities for science and human exploration," the agency added.

Starfish Space was a natural partner. The Seattle company plans to become a big player in the nascent field of satellite servicing, using its line of Otter craft to repair, refuel or deorbit other satellites for a variety of customers.

SSPICY marked Otter's spaceflight debut. The mission plan called for the 739-pound (335-kilogram) Otter 24C spacecraft to approach and inspect "up to four inoperable space objects of U.S. origin" over the course of a two-year mission, performing detailed visual inspections.

But Otter 24C never got the chance to perform any of these orbital rendezvous.

"While working through commissioning steps, Starfish eventually stopped receiving data from Otter 24C," the company said in a Nov. 3 X post.

"An investigation into the loss of communications has determined that fault protection on the satellite bus provided by [California company] Astro Digital had an error that turned off the radio and prevented re-establishing communications," Starfish added. "Starfish, NASA, and Astro Digital have concluded that Otter 24C is not recoverable."

The company further said that it's implementing fixes to reduce the chances that the problem will crop up in the future. And it stressed that Otter 24C's death will not be in vain.

"The work completed through Otter 24C will directly contribute to the success of future Otter missions, as Starfish continues developing the technologies and operations required to make satellite servicing a routine capability in orbit," Starfish said.

Otter Pup 2 is now operating as close as 25 meters away from @GilmourSpace's ElaraSat, fully autonomously. This vid contains imagery captured when we were separated by just 33.6 meters. We’ve demonstrated our ability to safely and precisely operate at very close range, executing intricate maneuvers, gathering detailed imagery, and testing the capabilities we’ll need for docking. With this progress, Otter Pup 2 has officially completed Characterize, the penultimate phase of its mission. That leaves just one phase left: attempting docking, and a chance to make history.October 27, 2026

The Seattle company has other work to do in LEO at the moment as well: Its Otter Pup 2 prototype craft is currently gearing up to conduct a historic docking of its own in LEO.

Otter Pup 2, which launched in June 2025, has been getting closer and closer to another private spacecraft, Gilmour Space's ElaraSat. Last week, the company announced that Otter Pup 2 got within a mere 82 feet (25 meters) of its target.

"With this progress, Otter Pup 2 has officially completed Characterize, the penultimate phase of its mission. That leaves just one phase left: attempting docking, and a chance to make history," Starfish Space said in an Oct. 27 X post.

Two private satellites have docked before, but only much higher above Earth, in geostationary orbit. Such a meetup has not yet happened in LEO.

#795. Five-inch-long beetle larvae are quietly destroying blueberry roots

North Carolina's blueberry growers are facing an emerging threat from a destructive beetle whose larvae feed underground, damaging plant roots and potentially killing blueberry bushes. Scientists have now identified the insect responsible, providing an important first step toward protecting crops from the pest.

A research team at North Carolina State University has confirmed that the culprit is Prionus imbricornus, a species of longhorn beetle distinguished by its long antennae. These wood-boring insects are becoming a growing concern for blueberry producers in the state.

Female beetles generally deposit their eggs in soil near the roots of hardwood trees. After hatching, the larvae feed on the roots, sometimes destroying enough tissue to kill the tree. The larvae can reach an impressive five inches in length, while the adult beetles do not feed.

A Decade-Old Mystery Beneath Blueberry Fields

North Carolina is the first state to document P. imbricornus feeding on blueberry bushes. However, signs of a similar problem have existed for years. Reports of unidentified Prionus larvae damaging blueberry roots date back to 2010, but researchers had struggled to determine which species was responsible.

Part of the challenge was the insects' underground habitat. Because the larvae remain near plant roots, they are difficult to locate and study. Making matters more complicated, larvae from different longhorn beetle species often look remarkably similar, making visual identification unreliable.

According to Kenneth Geisert, a graduate student in NC State's College of Agriculture and Life Sciences and lead author of the study, this uncertainty has made it difficult to develop appropriate pest control strategies.

"Before now, researchers often just assumed the species of Prionus on their commodities based on adult identification," Geisert said. "If that guess was incorrect, it could mean using a treatment strategy that did not line up with the problem and incorrectly associating species and their hosts. For instance, while P. imbricornus attacks roots, another type of longhorn beetle might attack the trunk of a tree, or dead branches. Without knowing which species of beetle you're dealing with and their ecology, incorrect management can cause adverse effects on non-target insects."

To identify the insects, the research team conducted fieldwork at six blueberry farms in North Carolina's Pender, Sampson, Bladen, and New Hanover counties.

The scientists installed black panel traps containing sex pheromones, chemical signals that attract adult beetles. After collecting the insects, they used a DNA identification technique known as genetic barcoding to determine the identity of larvae found in the fields.

This method examines short, standardized sections of DNA and compares them with reference sequences from known species. By matching genetic material from the unidentified larvae with DNA from adult Prionus beetles, the researchers could determine which species was present.

The analysis produced a 98 to 99 percent match with P. imbricornus, confirming the identity of the beetle responsible for the root damage.

A Growing Threat With No Approved Insecticides

Although identifying the pest represents an important breakthrough, it also highlights a serious challenge for blueberry growers.

Lorena Lopez, an assistant extension professor in NC State's Department of Entomology and Plant Pathology and a co-author of the study, explained that the discovery brings both encouraging and troubling news.

"On one hand, it's very important that we know which species we're dealing with," she said. "On the other, North Carolina was the first state to ever report Prionus infestation in blueberries, and there are no insecticides currently labeled against this pest in blueberries."

To help address this problem, Lopez has begun testing insecticides to determine which treatments might effectively control the beetles.

A major focus is finding the best time to apply treatments. By coordinating insecticide applications with the beetles' reproductive cycles, researchers hope to disrupt larval development before the insects can inflict extensive damage on blueberry roots.

If successful, this approach could give farmers a much-needed way to protect their crops against an emerging pest that has remained difficult to identify and manage for more than a decade.

The findings appear in the Journal of Integrated Pest Management in a paper titled "Prionus imbricornis (Coleoptera: Cerambycidae), an emerging pest in North Carolina blueberries." Gareth Powell, an assistant professor at NC State and director of the NCSU Insect Museum, also contributed to the research.

#794. Rosalía and Milo J Sweep the 2026 Latin Grammys: Full List of Winners

CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso, Jorge Drexler, Karol G and Grupo Frontera also won multiple awards on Thursday's (Nov. 12) ceremony.

With her widely acclaimed and eclectic LUX, Rosalía won the Latin Grammy for album of the year for the third time and took home, among other honors, song of the year for “La Perla,” alongside Yahritza y Su Esencia. It was an expected victory on a night that honored both major icons and fresh new voices of Latin music — such as Milo J, the Argentine newcomer who won the award for record of the year for “Niño” and took home three additional trophies, including best folk music album for La Vida Es Más Corta.

Rosalía also won awards for best pop song and best alternative music album, and LUX was further recognized for its recording engineering. But the honor that moved her to tears was, without a doubt, album of the year, which she received from Juanes — an artist who supported her very early in her career and whom she thanked for being there back when “there were only 100 people in a room in Madrid.”

“This is the third time I’ve won this award. If El Mal Querer was a dream, and Motomami was a bold gamble, then LUX has been a leap into the unknown,” said the Spanish superstar, referring to her winning albums of 2019 and 2022, respectively. “I believe it’s very important to speak your own truth — and for others to be able to speak theirs — and this record is mine. I thank God, and I thank my loved ones — my family and my friends. Thank-you for your love and for shaping me into who I am today. The truth is, I know I still have a lot to learn, and I’m certain that I likely haven’t even created my best work yet.”

Milo J, who at 19 years old earned six nominations for a project that pushed him well outside his comfort zone (urban music), also won for best urban/urban fusion performance for “Gil,” featuring Trueno, as well as for best recording package. He was also a contender for the album of the year award. “Coming from where I come from — from the trap genre — winning an award for folk music just blows my mind,” he said upon receiving the gramophone for best folk album. Milo spoke during the Latin Grammy Premiere — the non-televised ceremony held hours earlier, where the majority of the winners were announced — and used the moment to thank the producers and colleagues who contributed to the project.Among the winners announced during the ceremony, Karol G shone as she received the award for best urban music album for the third time — this time for Tropicoqueta.

“I’m going to be completely honest — thank God I’ve been here a few times before — but making Tropicoqueta meant so much to me, in ways many people can’t even imagine,” the Colombian star said. “I sat down with artists and musical masters I never dreamed I’d have the chance to collaborate or work with. I feel I’ve grown a great deal, both as a person and as an artist. Most importantly, I now have an album that I’m touring with, and when I perform these songs, I can see that people feel proud to be Latino. It’s beautiful to watch everyone singing along to salsa, merengue, reggaeton, bachata and mariachi — because that’s who we are: all of that, and so much more. So, thank-you.”

Among the veteran honorees were Jorge Drexler, Juanes and Fonseca, while first-time winners included the young Mexican artist Xavi and Brazilian superstar Anitta — who secured her first Latin Grammy after 12 nominations, winning best Portuguese language contemporary pop album for Equilibrivm.The coveted best new artist award went to Colombian Aria Vega, who was Billboard’s Latin Up-And-Comer artist of the month for July and recently participated in the Women’s Panel at Billboard Latin Music Week.

“I was reflecting on where I am in my life, and I thought of a college professor who once gave us an assignment to create something that described us. I put together some clippings that read ‘big dreams and good taste.’ Being here to receive this recognition is one of those ‘premium’ dreams,” she said upon accepting her award.

CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso, the sensational Argentine duo that took home five awards during their Latin Grammy debut last year, won best Latin electronic music performance for “Beto’s Horns – Fred Remix” with Fred Again..; best pop/rock song for “Hasta Jesús Tuvo Un Mal Día” with Sting; and best long form music video for FREE SPIRITS (The Film).

Other early winners included Luis Enrique, Grupo Frontera, Camila Fernández and Bobby Pulido — the latter having recently been elected to the House of Representatives for the Democrats.

“I want to tell you that I’m retiring from music, and I’m leaving with so much gratitude,” he said while accepting his trophy. “I’m so, so proud to be from Texas and to be Tejano and to represent this music. Tejano music is in very good hands; we have so much talent — young talent like [fellow nominees] Jay Pérez, Destiny Navaira, everyone who’s here. I love you all, and I’ll see you soon, because we need to represent and we need to get to work to use our voices for something else.”

Among the big surprises of the everning, Venezuelan newcomer Sara Schell took home the award for songwriter of the year, besting heavyweights such as Edgar Barrera — who led the list of nominees with 10 nods and went on to win his fourth producer of the year award.

“I’m shaking—wow,” said the 23-year-old songwriter as she accepted her golden gramophone. “My name is Sara Schell; I’m from Barquisimeto, Venezuela, and this award is for my family. And when I say ‘my family,’ I don’t just mean my mom and dad… I also mean my friends and my team. Thank you for all the support; thank you for all the love.”

Daddy Yankee — the Latin Recording Academy’s 2026 Person of the Year, honored a day before by his peers at a traditional gala — also won best urban song alongside Bizarrap for “Daddy Yankee: Bzrp Music Sessions, Vol. 0/66.”

The 27th Annual Latin Grammy Awards ceremony, hosted by singer and actress Roselyn Sánchez, was broadcast live from Las Vegas on TelevisaUnivision platforms. Performers included Rosalía, Karol G, Anitta, Elena Rose, Juanes, Milo J, Mon Laferte and many others.

#793. Scientists accidentally solve a chemistry mystery that lasted 60 years

A chemistry challenge that had frustrated researchers for more than 60 years has finally been overcome. Scientists at the University of Würzburg in Germany have discovered a way to produce and isolate oxoboranes, a group of unusual molecules that were long considered too unstable to study under ordinary laboratory conditions.

The breakthrough, published in Nature Chemistry, was led by Professor Holger Braunschweig and his team, with computational support from researchers led by Professor Ashwini K. Phukan at Tezpur University in India. Their findings reveal a surprisingly straightforward way to create these elusive compounds, potentially opening new possibilities for molecular chemistry.

Boron is an element that rarely forms triple bonds, a type of chemical connection in which two atoms share three pairs of electrons. For more than 15 years, Braunschweig has focused on overcoming this limitation and creating molecules containing unusual bonds involving boron.

His laboratory has already achieved several important milestones. In 2012, the team reported the first molecule containing a triple bond between two boron atoms. Another breakthrough followed in 2025, when the researchers produced the first neutral molecule featuring a triple bond between boron and carbon.

One major challenge remained among the elements in the first row of the periodic table's p-block. Researchers had yet to isolate stable organic oxoboranes, molecules characterized by a triple bond between boron and oxygen.

Chemists around the world had been pursuing these compounds since at least the early 1960s. Over the decades, scientists working in both organic and inorganic chemistry had managed to detect and trap oxoboranes under extreme conditions. Other experiments provided indirect evidence of their existence, and researchers succeeded in creating several related derivatives. However, obtaining stable examples that could be isolated and examined remained an unsolved problem.

An Unexpected Reaction Produces Elusive Molecules

The long-awaited breakthrough emerged from experiments that initially appeared to be heading in a different direction.

Two doctoral students at the University of Würzburg, Lukas Lubczyk and Christian Markl, were independently investigating reactions between a compound known as a diboracumulene and various ketones, which are commonly used chemicals in organic synthesis.

Both researchers noticed something unusual. Instead of producing only the outcomes they might have expected, the reactions generated distinctive orange or yellow solids.

"The discovery was a pleasant surprise. I never thought the diboracumulene would react the way it did, let alone with multiple different, simple substrates. And when Christian came to me with his compound, I knew we were onto something," says Lukas Lubczyk.

What made the results particularly remarkable was that oxoboranes emerged as the main products of these reactions, even though several other chemical outcomes had appeared more likely. After decades of unsuccessful efforts to isolate such molecules, the researchers had found that they could form unexpectedly from reactions involving relatively simple starting materials.

Braunschweig described just how surprising the discovery was to scientists familiar with the long-standing challenge.

"Nearly everybody in the field had given up on oxoboranes, as they were thought to be just too unstable to be isolated. So we were stunned to see them spontaneously form in these reactions and stick around long enough that we could study them," says Holger Braunschweig.

Using their newly discovered method, the scientists successfully prepared three different oxoboranes. The fact that the approach worked with multiple compounds suggests that it could provide access to a much wider range of these previously difficult to isolate molecules.

The team is now investigating how broadly the technique can be applied. Beyond producing additional oxoboranes, the researchers hope to determine whether similar strategies could help them create other elusive compounds involving elements throughout the periodic table.

The discovery not only resolves a problem that challenged chemists for more than six decades but also demonstrates how unexpected chemical reactions can reveal possibilities that researchers once considered beyond reach.

International Research Collaboration and Funding

The findings were published through a collaboration between the Würzburg research team and the group led by Professor Ashwini K. Phukan at Tezpur University (India), whose computational research helped support the work.

Funding was provided by the German Research Foundation (DFG), the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD), and the Department of Science & Technology (DST) of India.

They say all good things come to those who wait… and WAIT. Well, the wait for "Robopocalypse" fans might finally be over, as Oscar winners Ron Howard and Akiva Goldsman have announced they're working on a TV adaptation.

It does seem like an eternity since news first broke that Portland-based New York Times bestselling author Daniel H. Wilson’s "Robopocalypse" (Doubleday, 2011) was bought by Steven Spielberg’s DreamWorks SKG for a sci-fi spectacle, with Drew Goddard ("The Martian") brought in to pen the screenplay.

That was back in 2009, and since then the story of a rogue AI named Archos and a hearty band of indigenous people in America’s heartland battling to save humanity from extinction has been placed on Hollywood’s back burner. After numerous stalled starts and director Michael Bay getting involved in 2018, "Robopocalypse" was quietly powered down due to script issues, filmmaker scheduling conflicts, and the enormous budget required.

But now we have been blessed with the news, first broken by The Hollywood Reporter, that Ron Howard ("Apollo 13," "The Da Vinci Code") and Akiva Goldsman ("A Beautiful Mind," "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds") have taken up the mantle of this chilling sci-fi project to develop as a new TV series. And what timing, just as AI fever has gripped the planet with paranoia centered around our eventual robot overlords.

"'Robopocalypse' has all the scale and suspense of a major action story, but what drew me to it are the thought-provoking themes and humanity at its center," Ron Howard shared in a statement.

The cover of 2011's smash sci-fi hit Robopocalypse by Daniel H. Wilson

The cover of the 2014 sequel Robogenesis by Daniel H. Wilson

"Daniel created a future that feels both startling and increasingly plausible, with characters who must figure out what connects us when the technology we rely on turns against us. I am also thrilled to work with Akiva again. We have shared some incredibly meaningful creative experiences, and this feels like the right story to bring us back together."

As a PhD graduate of Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute and a future king of the techno-thriller, Wilson was the ideal writer to bring this frightening story to life, and a 2014 sequel titled "Robogenesis" was equally gripping.

The prolific, award-winning writer has since set up a multitude of other Hollywood projects spawned from his catalog of works, including "Amped," "The Clockwork Dynasty," the authorized sequel to Michael Crichton's "The Andromeda Strain," "The Andromeda Evolution," and his 2025 alien invasion novel "Hole in the Sky," still alive at Netflix.

Howard's Imagine Entertainment will partner with Akiva Goldsman's Weed Road Pictures on this episodic adaptation, with Howard attached to direct the pilot episode and Goldsman serving as series showrunner.

"Robopocalypse" marks a creative reunion for the distinguished creators, following their collaborations on "A Beautiful Mind," "Cinderella Man," "The Da Vinci Code," and "Angels & Demons." Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment is slated to executive produce the ambitious show alongside Imagine's Brian Grazer and Jeb Brody and Weed's Rachel Wizenberg and Greg Lessans.

It's too early to tell which streaming service the "Robopocalypse" TV show will be attached to yet. Hopefully the pilot episode wows one of the big names, and we can finally see the "Robopocalypse" adaptation of our dreams.

In the meantime, we'd recommend checking out the original book by Daniel H. Wilson.

Not far into our future, the dazzling technology that runs our world turns against us. Controlled by a childlike—yet massively powerful—artificial intelligence known as Archos, the global network of machines on which our world has grown dependent suddenly becomes an implacable, deadly foe.

#791. Scientists discover that a clogged filter could revolutionize oil refining

Researchers have developed a surprisingly simple way to separate crude oil without heating it, potentially transforming one of the world's most energy-intensive industrial processes. The breakthrough uses an inexpensive membrane that could significantly reduce the energy required for oil refining while lowering operating costs and carbon emissions.

The international research effort was led by Professor Dong-Yeun Koh at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, known as KAIST, in collaboration with Professor Ryan Lively's research group at Georgia Tech. KAIST(President Kwang Hyung Lee) announced that the team had successfully demonstrated a membrane capable of separating crude oil at room temperature. The findings were published in Nature, one of the world's leading scientific journals.

Crude oil is essential for far more than gasoline and other transportation fuels. It also supplies the raw materials used to manufacture plastics, packaging, clothing, and numerous everyday products. Because refining costs affect the prices of these materials, making the process more efficient could have widespread economic and environmental benefits.

Why Traditional Crude Oil Refining Requires So Much Energy

For more than a century, oil refineries have relied heavily on distillation to separate crude oil into useful components. The process involves heating oil to temperatures above 350 °C, turning portions of it into vapor, and then cooling those vapors to collect different fractions.

This approach requires an enormous amount of energy. Worldwide, crude oil distillation consumes approximately 1,100 terawatt-hours (TWh) annually. That is comparable to the combined yearly electricity production of roughly 130 continuously operating nuclear power plants, each with a capacity of about one gigawatt.

The massive energy demand makes distillation a major contributor to both fuel consumption and greenhouse gas emissions within the refining industry. Meanwhile, growing economic pressures across global petrochemical markets have increased interest in technologies that can separate oil more efficiently.

Membranes have emerged as a promising alternative because they can separate substances without requiring the extreme temperatures used in conventional distillation. However, previous designs have faced significant obstacles.

Traditionally, researchers have assumed that effective molecular separation requires a membrane covered with an extremely thin, specialized coating. Although these coatings can provide the necessary precision, they are expensive to produce and can develop defects when manufactured on a large scale. These limitations have made widespread industrial adoption difficult.

A Surprising Discovery Turns Clogged Filters Into an Advantage

The KAIST and Georgia Tech researchers approached the problem differently. Rather than adding a complicated coating, they used a bare membrane made from porous polyacrylonitrile (PAN), an inexpensive, chemically stable polymer already commonly used as a supporting material in industrial filtration systems.

What happened when crude oil passed through the membrane was unexpected.

As the oil flowed through its pores, heavier hydrocarbon molecules accumulated along the inner walls. This buildup gradually reduced the size of the openings, producing extremely narrow channels measuring less than 2 nanometers across.

In effect, the crude oil helped create the microscopic pathways needed to separate its own components.

These naturally formed channels allowed lighter oil fractions, including naphtha, gasoline, and kerosene, to pass through quickly while preventing heavier substances from traveling through the membrane as easily.

The discovery was especially surprising because the buildup of material inside membrane pores, known as fouling, is normally considered a serious problem. Fouling typically reduces filtration performance and requires cleaning or replacement. In this case, however, the same phenomenon made the membrane highly effective at separating different molecules.

The results were impressive. The uncoated PAN membrane achieved crude oil permeation rates approximately 23 times higher than those reported for previous leading crude oil separation membranes. It also continued operating with stable performance for 28 consecutive days.

Professor Ryan Lively (Georgia Tech) commented: "One of the key challenges facing membrane systems for crude oil separation was the low productivities of the membrane units -- the PAN membranes with their surprising separation mechanism -- dramatically increase the productivity of the membrane unit, to the point where industry should seriously consider adopting the technology."

New Membrane Could Cut Oil Refining Energy Use by Nearly a Third

One of the technology's biggest advantages is that refineries would not necessarily need to replace their existing equipment to use it.

The membrane could instead be installed as a modular filtration system that processes crude oil before it enters conventional distillation equipment. This would reduce the amount of work required during the heating and separation stages while allowing facilities to continue using much of their current infrastructure.

Computer simulations suggest that incorporating the membrane into the refining process could deliver substantial improvements. Energy consumption could fall by 31.6%, while carbon dioxide emissions could decrease by 37.6%. The same calculations projected a 20.7% reduction in cooling water consumption and a 36% decrease in operating costs.

The potential environmental benefits could be considerable if the technology were adopted widely.

Researchers estimate that implementing the system throughout Korea's refining and petrochemical industries could prevent approximately 10 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions each year. That is roughly equivalent to the annual emissions produced by four million vehicles powered by internal combustion engines.

These savings are projections based on process simulations rather than reductions already demonstrated across operating refineries. Nevertheless, the findings suggest that membrane filtration could become a practical way to improve the efficiency of existing facilities.

Although crude oil separation was the main focus of the research, the same technology could eventually be useful in several other industries.

One potential application involves treating pyrolysis oil produced when waste plastics are broken down for recycling. The membranes could also help recover solvents used in battery manufacturing, purify pharmaceutical compounds, and improve biofuel production.

The broader opportunity lies in using complex liquid mixtures to help form the tiny filtration channels needed to separate their components. This approach could provide a more affordable and versatile alternative to conventional membranes that require precisely manufactured surface coatings.

Professor Dong-Yeun Koh of KAIST said, "This study reveals a new scientific principle in which a membrane interacts with a complex mixture and spontaneously forms its own separation channels. Working with real crude oil supplied by HD Hyundai Oilbank allowed us to validate the technology under conditions relevant to industrial operation."

The use of actual crude oil was an important part of the research because it allowed the team to examine how the membrane performed with the complicated mixture of hydrocarbons found in industrial feedstocks.

Before the technology can be deployed more widely, the researchers plan to improve membrane production at larger scales and establish its reliability during extended operation.

Professor Jae W. Lee of KAIST, a co-corresponding author of the study, added, "By advancing large-area membrane modularization and long-term operational reliability, we hope to broaden the adoption of membrane-based processes throughout the refining and petrochemical industries."

Dr. Jihoon Choi and Dr. Hyeokjun Seo of KAIST, the study's co-first authors, said, "Our goal is to precisely control this spontaneous pore-constriction phenomenon and develop it into a membrane platform applicable to the entire refining process. We also aim to expand the technology to plastic recycling, biofuel purification, and other sustainable chemical processes that support carbon neutrality."

The research received support from Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT through the Basic Research Program for Outstanding Early-Career Researchers and the Engineering Research Center (ERC) Program.

#790. Dolly Parton Sings ‘Her Heart Out’ on Posthumous U2 Collaboration ‘Torn’: Stream It Now

Co-written by U2, Parton and Snow Patrol's Johnny McDaid, "Torn" is the country great's last recorded vocal performance.

Dolly Parton always gave it her all across her glittering, extraordinary career. At the stroke of midnight, the country music icon reminded us of what we’re sorely missing with the release of “Torn,” Parton’s posthumous collaboration with U2. Explore Bono Dolly Parton U2 See latest videos, charts and news

The duet between Dolly and U2 frontman Bono is the closing song on Carnaval De Luz (which translates to “Carnival of Light”), the Irish rock band’s sixteenth and latest studio album. Related Aria Vega Wins Best New Artist at the 2026 Latin Grammys: 'Dreams Know No Fear' On Winning First Latin Grammy, Camila Fernández Thanks Expectant Baby for 'Strength to be Here' 50 Cent Trolls Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's Affair With 'P.I.M.P.' Music Video AI Deepfake: 'Jensen Don't Sweat It'

Co-written by U2, Parton and Snow Patrol‘s Johnny McDaid, “Torn” is the country great’s last recorded vocal performance, and it connects the full 24-track deluxe version of the project, followed in sequence by the surprise-release EPs Days of Ash and Easter Lily, as a double album.

Dolly pulls it together, to create a spiritual whole. “You sense a border crossing,” Bono remarks in a statement. “And so you move from the south into the north, and you have Dolly Parton singing to you as you cross the border.”

Carnaval De Luz is the first album of new material from U2 in nine years. To celebrate its release, Island Records shares several versions of the country-tinged “Torn,” including the “Kent Wells Version” and the “T Bone Burnett Take,” all of them featuring the unmistakable voice of Dolly.

Speaking ahead of its release, Bono told Rolling Stone that the recording was, admittedly, almost too difficult for him to hear.

“When she got ill, she got out of her bed to sing this song,” Bono remarked. “And you can hear that. And I can’t even listen to it now.”

Parton recorded her vocals for “Torn” in June, just two months before her passing. Bono was blown away by her talents. “She sang her heart out,” he told RS, “and I cannot believe that’s an 80-year-old woman.”

Parton approved the final mix before her passing Aug. 25 at 80 from a brief battle with cancer.

“It’s very moving to have had these intimacies with such a figure,” Bono explained to Rolling Stone. “The fact that they’re not there now, in any way you can call back, other than through her songs, is very sobering.”

Carnaval De Luz drops 50 years after drummer Larry Mullen Jr. pinned a handwritten notice to the message board of Mount Temple Comprehensive School in Dublin, with the fateful message: “Drummer Seeks Musicians To Form Band.”

What happened next is the stuff of legend.

With their political hearts exposed on their collective sleeves, Bono, The Edge, Mullen and Adam Clayton would become arguably the world’s biggest band in the second half of the 1980s, a crown they managed to wear well into the ‘90s despite the explosion of grunge, indie, alternative rock, hip-hop and electronic dance music.

The band has sold 175 million albums, according to Island Records, and bagged 22 Grammy Awards. Along the way, they landed 34 songs on the Billboard Hot 100, including two leaders, along with eight No. 1s on the Billboard 200 chart. Induction into the Rock And Roll Hall of Fame came in 2005.

U2 had the honors of being the first band to play the Sphere in Las Vegas, which they inaugurated in September 2023 with the residency, U2:UV Achtung Baby Live at Sphere.

According to reps, the fourpiece is currently working on plans to translate the new album for Carnaval De Luz presents: The Greatest Show On Earth World Tour, a live tour in 2027.

#789. Novel CRISPR therapy is poised to gain first FDA approval to alter genes inside the body

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

The Cas9 protein together with RNA and DNA (orange; artist’s illustration). A new therapy uses the CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing system to treat a rare genetic disease called hereditary angioedema.Credit: Alfred Pasieka/Science Photo Library

A pioneering therapy that edits genes inside a recipient’s body continues to be effective four years after treatment, according to data released by its developer, Intellia Therapeutics.

The therapy, named lonvoguran ziclumeran (lonvo-z), was designed to treat one form of a genetic disorder that causes episodes of painful and potentially dangerous swelling in the throat and other parts of the body. Lonvo-z deploys the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing system to disable the gene that produces prekallikrein, a protein made in the liver that promotes blood-vessel leakage.

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

Bigger than CRISPR? A guide to the latest genome editors

Intellia, headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has applied for approval of lonvo-z to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which is expected to issue a decision by 10 March. If approved, the therapy will become the world’s first CRISPR medicine to be delivered directly inside the body, or in vivo, John Leonard, Intellia’s chief executive, told investors on 12 November. Currently, the only CRISPR therapy approved by the FDA is performed on cells that have first been removed from the body and are subsequently re-infused.

For people with the condition, hereditary angioedema, the gene-editing approach could offer relief from a lifetime of juggling medications to prevent and treat swelling attacks, says Jonathan Bernstein, a hereditary angioedema specialist at the University of Cincinnati in Ohio and an investigator on a lonvo-z trial. “It’s very reassuring,” he says of the four-year data. “That’s what you’re supposed to see.”

The only approved CRISPR therapy is Casgevy, a treatment for two genetic blood disorders, sickle cell anemia and ß-thalassemia. To create a dose of Casgevy, physicians first remove blood stem cells from the recipient, then send them off for gene editing. The edited cells are infused back into the recipient.

The therapy must be made anew for each person, adding time, cost, and complexity. The recipient also has to undergo harsh chemotherapy treatment to make room for the edited cells.

CRISPR makes enhanced cancer-fighting immune cells inside mice

CRISPR makes enhanced cancer-fighting immune cells inside mice

In vivo gene-editing approaches aim to sidestep these concerns by editing genes directly in the body. Lonvo-z, for example, consists of fatty particles that encase mRNA encoding CRISPR-Cas9 components. The particles are infused into the blood and taken up by the liver, where prekallikrein is produced. The procedure takes one day.

In vivo gene editing can introduce other safety concerns, however. The therapy affords no opportunity to screen out cells with unwanted edits at other locations in the genome, or in other organs. Recipients might also have harmful immune responses to the treatment.

Last year, the FDA placed a clinical hold on two other in vivo studies sponsored by Intellia after a participant — an older man with other health conditions — developed liver damage and died after receiving a CRISPR treatment. The FDA lifted the hold this year after requiring added safety measures.
