#762. ‘The Body’ Creator on the Dance Team’s Sexuality, What Happened to Grace and Whether God Is Real

SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for “The Body,” now streaming on Netflix.

If you’re looking for clear answers about whether or not God is real in the world of “The Body” — Netflix’s spooky new drama series about mass hysteria originating from a Catholic school dance team — you’re not going to find them.

“If we ever fully defined it, it would break the rule of the show,” says creator Quinn Shephard. “The show is meant to mimic faith, so there’s people who believe, there’s people who don’t and there’s people in the middle, like me, who are like, ‘I don’t know.’”

But regardless of whether it’s the big man upstairs or just some devious teenage girls pulling the strings, “The Body” has a lot to say about faith and its role in the lives of young and sometimes queer girls. Shephard is a proud lesbian who was raised in the church and has stepped away from it without fully rejecting it, and the show’s up-and-down relationship with God is a product of that.

At the beginning of “The Body,” a devout Catholic named Grace (Sofia Wylie) is the clear standout at dance team tryouts, much to the chagrin of some of the team’s more senior members, who roll their eyes at her rule-following innocence. Thus, she’s put through a bit of hazing: At a Halloween party at an abandoned convent, she’s pressured to take Ecstasy by Elise (Sara Boustany), the team’s co-captain and resident badass, as everyone jokingly perform a ritual meant to sacrifice her soul to the devil. But the devil doesn’t seem to know that they’re joking. Anya (Kristina Bogic), who is Elise’s co-captain and the most popular girl in school, notices that Grace has wandered off alone. Alongside Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros), an awkward new girl who got rejected from the team in favor of Grace, she finds Grace on the ground, convulsing until she passes out. Anya and Lisbeth decide to take her to a hospital, but on the way, Grace appears to die. Because Anya supplied the Ecstasy, she’s terrified she’ll get in trouble. Lisbeth sees this as her way onto the dance team and into Anya’s good graces, and takes charge. They take Grace’s body back to her own house and tuck her into bed, then use Grace’s phone to text a friend that she got home safe, giving themselves plausible deniability. But at the end of the first episode, Grace takes a breath.

She doesn’t wake all the way up, though, and spends the rest of the season in a coma as the dance team is wracked with guilt about the Ecstasy, which they don’t confess about. Needing support from the only other person who knows what happened, Anya brings Lisbeth onto the dance team to take Grace’s place, which intensifies the conflict between Anya and Elise. The two best friends are clearly in love with each other, and had been fooling around sexually at the party, but Anya insists that she’s straight and loyal to her boyfriend, Steven (Orlando Norman). Frustrated by Anya’s new closeness to Lisbeth, and with latent suspicion about Anya’s role in what happened to Grace, Elise fakes a spiritual experience, shrieking in front of the whole school that she’s having a vision of Grace. But everyone on the team — except Anya and Lisbeth, of course — buys into it. One by one, they begin faking their own visions. Soon, the whole town starts to believe that Grace is all-powerful, chosen by God to perform healing miracles from her apparent deathbed. People gather on her family’s lawn to worship her.

Lisbeth is delighted, using her relationship with Anya to increase her social standing at school and to protect her brother, Leo (Jackson Kelly), who at one point drew suspicion because of his crush on (and lewd drawings of) Grace. But eventually, Elise pieces together the truth, forcing Anya to confess to Father Franklin (Nnamdi Asomugha), the school principal and pastor. At that exact moment, though, Grace finally wakes up. Weakly, she whispers, “I’m God.”

Shepherd spoke with Variety about Catholicism, lesbian camp and who-slash-what God is. Related Stories MCU Surprise: ‘VisionQuest’ Finale Teases the Return of [SPOILER] in ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Oscar Predictions: Film Editing — ‘You Can See Everything’ Looks to Crash a Race of Past Winners and Become the Third Documentary Ever Nominated

I definitely put so much of myself into those two characters, and also some of my close friends who let me use their stories. I do find the era really interesting, because it wasn’t like being gay was illegal, or like you’re guaranteed to get disowned, but it was definitely not good. And it felt like the biggest threat was to your femininity, and your social standing as normal or cool. I didn’t go to high school in 2004; I was in high school a little later than that. But pre-smartphones and pre-gay marriage being legalized, that was a very specific era. Being lesbian felt like a bit. I remember my friends and I doing so many bits where we’d “pretend” to be gay for each other. It’s not that it wasn’t being talked about; it’s that it wasn’t cool. I was like, “I can’t be gay.” This is going to sound so bad, but I think I thought I had to be butch. I didn’t want to, like, get a short haircut and start wearing rainbow knee socks.

For Anya, that’s her worst fear. She’s not ready. She’s quite high femme, and on the top of the social hierarchy, and she’s like, “Oh my God. Not only am I going to threaten that, but I have to give up on all these ideas of what my life is going to be? Are people going to act differently around me in the locker room? Am I going to lose my girlhood? Am I going to lose my status?” And we talked a lot in the room about how much Catholicism plays into Anya’s fears — it is a fear that she’s going to go to hell, but it’s not the main fear. Certainly, a piece of her shame comes from Catholicism, but I think it’s more interesting and more relatable to more people that she’s equally afraid, if not more afraid, that she’s just gonna lose her identity.

Because of that, even though she also has a lot of kindness to her, she does a lot of really fucked up things. I wanted to make a very unsanitized, messy first queer love story. I was seeing too many shows where the characters are gay and it’s totally fine and no one has a problem with it. Like, there’s the parent who’s a little homophobic, and then there’s one conversation where they’re like, “Actually, I love you, honey.” No. It’s messy as hell. And you do some crazy stuff that you look back on, like, “Why did I do that?” I really wanted to give that to Anya and Elise.

I like to joke that with the amount of queer women involved in making the show, the core ethos and tone is so inherently like lesbian camp and a lesbian sense of humor. That even applies to the fact that there’s a lot of really lovable men in the story. The men are kind of innocent, and that’s from a lot of the women working on the show being like, “With the men that I dated, it wasn’t their fault that I wasn’t into them. It was me and my journey, and God, what I put that guy through!” Everyone in the show is linked to that twisted sense of humor and trying to turn shame and trauma into comedy. But we’ve got stuff to play with in Season 2 in terms of queer characters.

I actually really like that people have debates about Lisbeth. Because to make her relationship with Anya about sexuality would almost be too simple. I think it’s way bigger than that. Lisbeth’s character isn’t driven by sexuality, almost at all. She’s more driven by survival. She’s a child of trauma, and she’s got some slightly asexual and sociopathic tendencies coming out, but I don’t think that’s necessarily who she is forever. It’s more that that’s where we meet her, because she’s in survival mode.

I love Lisbeth. I don’t think she’s inherently bad. I just think she’s opportunistic in the first season, and too smart for her own good. It’s almost frustrating to her how ahead of other people her brain is. She’s definitely a bit on the spectrum. She struggles with social cues, but she’s brilliant, and she can’t help but see opportunities and strategies. For me, the lovable part of her is that she can strategize a takeover. She can play three-dimensional chess. She is starting mass hysteria to protect her brother and gain access to the dance team.

But at the end of the day, she doesn’t know how to act like a normal high-school girl at a party. She can’t do it. She tries so hard, and she literally studies it like gospel, but she can’t get there, and I think that’s so human. Sometimes it feels like there’s a way to study something and get there, but you can’t because that’s not how life works. And she had such a profound relationship with religion when she was younger that she lost. It’s like she’s searching for something that profound again, and when she finds it, she’s literally not going to be stopped. She’s a dog with a bone. If she wants to be on that dance team, she’s getting on that dance team no matter what, even if she has to hide a body. She’s getting there.

I think it’s both. It changes. There are scenes where she’s like, “I’m so enamored with this girl. I wish I could be just like her. I don’t know if I want to be with her, be like her, be around her or be inside her skin. I don’t know. I’m just obsessed.” And then there’s other times where she’s like, “This girl is on my nerves.” It’s very hard for Lisbeth when Anya is like, “Why are you not freaking out?” And she’s like, “I am, but this is how I freak out.” She doesn’t understand Anya, but there are moments, like when she sees that Anya’s working on her dance team jacket, and Anya’s letting her into her closet, that’s like the happiest day of Lisbeth’s life. She’s like, “I finally have a friend, and I’m so happy.” Does she have some ulterior motives? Yeah. But there’s also a really wholesome motive in there too. She wants a friend.

Maddie’s quite an earnest character. I don’t feel like she’s ever purposefully deceiving. She really struggles with the lies that the girls are telling. One of the writers, Lily Houghton, told a story about how she lost both her parents. They were very beloved, and so many people came up to her, like, “Your dad came to me in a dream. I saw your mom yesterday, and she came with messages.” And she got to the point where she was like, “I don’t want to hear people’s stories about my parents visiting them, because if they’re going to visit someone, why would they not visit me?” And it was such a personal, vivid story. We were all so moved. It’s so human to still feel like a kid, like, “I feel like it would be me,” and also the bigger picture of people claiming someone else’s loss. So we baked a lot of that into Maddie’s desire to see Grace, and I would say she ends the show believing. And that gets validated, because she’s the one who says that when everyone confesses, that’s when Grace is going to wake up, and then that happens. She’s going to be telling anyone who will listen that she got a prophecy. I think she’s like,”My best friend is God, and it’s cool.”

The rule that we have internally is that the show’s perspective on the supernatural needs to mimic a relationship with faith. So you can choose how you want to view the events that are presented. For every supernatural theory, there needs to be a countertheory, and the audience needs to be empowered to decide which show they’re watching and which character they align with. When people are like, “What is happening for you?” I’m like, “I don’t know! I don’t know what happens after we die. I don’t know the meaning of life. I don’t know exactly what God is.” The people making the show still have questions, so the show still has questions, and that’s the rule.

To me, that’s the same as being like, “On Earth, is there a God? Or is there not?” It is impossible for me to answer. And have a similar attitude with the show. The show exists in the unknown space. With the ending, there are clear supernatural and grounded, scientific theories that can explain that, and that’s the crux of the question we go into the next season with.

It’s part of why I love and gravitate towards spiritual journalism — journalism that follows people’s unexplainable events. I like material without an agenda, that’s just like, “This has happened to this many people. We don’t know what it means.” People say that when you have a near-death experience, your brain fires your neurons and it gives you this crazy hallucination. And then there’s this camp of people who says you’re really seeing the afterlife. But, literally, we can’t know. Unless we die. So I don’t know! If we ever fully defined it, it would break the rule of the show. The show is meant to mimic faith, so there’s people who believe, there’s people who don’t and there’s people in the middle, like me, who are like, “I don’t know.”

We always knew the ending going into the first season, and I think that moment is so fun because it provokes exactly the conversation that we’ve been having in the writers’ room. We hear Michael say that people can hear things in comas sometimes, so there’s a part of you that goes, “Maybe she’s been hearing everyone talking about these theories, and she knows.” We also have heard countless stories in life about people in comas, or people who have died and come back, who have these crazy visions. Did she experience the afterlife? Has she changed? Did something happen to her soul? Is it supernatural? And also, since she’s waking up from a coma, is she going to remember what she says? People say and do crazy things when they’re waking up from comas they have no memory of. The fact that people are excited to discuss their theory on what that ending means is exactly what I want. Without saying too much, it’s a perfect encapsulation of what we’d like to do with the next season.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

#761. Human bodies produce 2 billion metric tons of CO2 a year just by staying alive

Every human body produces carbon dioxide simply by converting food into energy. Although the amount released by one person may seem small, the combined output of billions of people adds up to an enormous quantity.

A new study led by the University of Bath estimates that carbon dioxide production from human metabolism increased by 74% between 1985 and 2015, reaching 2.05 billion metric tons annually. The researchers found that the dramatic rise was primarily the result of population growth, rather than a substantial increase in how much CO2 each person produces.

The findings could help scientists better understand the global carbon cycle, which describes how carbon moves between the atmosphere, living organisms, oceans, and land. By measuring humanity's contribution more accurately, researchers hope to improve predictions about how well efforts to reduce carbon emissions will work.

Why Human CO2 Emissions Are Different From Fossil Fuels

Despite the enormous numbers, the researchers emphasize that the carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism is fundamentally different from the emissions generated by burning fossil fuels.

When people breathe out CO2, most of that carbon originally came from the food they consumed. Plants absorbed it from the atmosphere relatively recently, meaning it is already circulating through the natural carbon cycle.

Burning coal, oil, and natural gas is different. These fuels contain carbon that has remained trapped underground for millions of years. Burning them releases that long-stored carbon into the atmosphere, adding to the amount of CO2 circulating through the Earth's climate system.

The new research, published in The Lancet Planetary Health, was led by Professor Javier Gonzalez of the University of Bath's Centre for Exercise, Nutrition and Metabolism.

The team calculated that global CO2 production from human metabolism climbed from 1.18 billion metric tons in 1985 to 2.05 billion metric tons in 2015. More than 60% of that increase could be attributed to the growing number of people worldwide.

"We all produce carbon dioxide simply by turning food into energy, but until now we haven't had a good idea how much that adds up to worldwide.

"What we've found is that the increase is mainly because there are more of us. This gives scientists one more piece of the puzzle when working out where carbon comes from and where it goes. Ultimately, this information can help scientists more accurately predict how effective carbon reduction strategies may be."

How Scientists Measured Humanity's CO2 Production

To estimate how much carbon dioxide people generate, the researchers analyzed thousands of measurements collected from individuals across the human lifespan, from infants to older adults.

These measurements provided information about the CO2 produced by the body during ordinary daily activities. The team then combined those findings with worldwide population figures and body weight data to calculate how human metabolic CO2 production had changed over time.

The results showed that population growth was the dominant factor behind the 74% increase. Changes in the amount of carbon dioxide generated by individual people played a much smaller role.

Accurately measuring this process is important because human metabolism contributes to the continuous movement of carbon through the environment. Its influence on local carbon measurements can be especially noticeable in densely populated cities and urban areas, where large numbers of people live and work close together.

Understanding these contributions can help researchers develop more complete carbon budgets, which track the sources, movements, and destinations of carbon within the Earth's systems.

Scientists Stress That Breathing Is Not Driving Climate Change

Although the study reveals a surprisingly large amount of CO2 production, its findings should not be interpreted as evidence that human breathing is a major cause of global warming.

The researchers are not recommending that people reduce their physical activity or change their diets to lower the carbon dioxide produced by their bodies. Instead, the goal is to make scientific measurements and calculations of the global carbon cycle more accurate.

Distinguishing between carbon dioxide produced through natural biological processes and carbon released by burning fossil fuels is essential for understanding the planet's changing climate.

Professor Gonzalez emphasized this distinction:

"The important thing is that the carbon dioxide we breathe out is not the same as burning fossil fuels. We're not saying that breathing is driving climate change.

"What this study does is give us a much clearer picture of how much CO2 people produce around the world, and how that is changing as the population grows. This understanding can help improve the accuracy predictions of carbon reduction programs."

By establishing a clearer picture of humanity's metabolic CO2 production, the researchers have provided another piece of information scientists can use to track global carbon movements and evaluate strategies for reducing emissions.

While rivals announce increasingly expensive smart telescopes, ZWO’s new Seestar S30 Plus makes galaxy and nebula photography surprisingly affordable.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As rival makers announce increasingly ambitious smart telescopes, ZWO has taken a different approach. Its new Seestar S30 Plus launched today and is available for $474 from Seestar’s website and Amazon, just in time for Christmas. Better still, we’ve been using it for a month and can bring you a first look.

Announced a few months after the flagship Seestar S50 Pro and replacing the now-discontinued Seestar S30, the new Seestar S30 Plus retains its 30mm aperture and compact chassis, but upgrades to four-element apochromatic optics with extra-low dispersion (ED) glass and two 3.7-megapixel cameras.

It has a 1.2-inch (30 mm) aperture, two 3.7 MP cameras and four-element apochromatic optics bundled into a compact build.

Both produce 1,440 x 2,560-pixel images, while a much-improved 43.5-degree wide-angle camera can capture the Milky Way, constellations, star trails and nightscapes. Built-in filters, a mosaic mode and equatorial (EQ) tracking add considerable deep-sky astrophotography potential.

For a telescope weighing just 3.64 lbs (1.65 kg), it’s impressive. It easily fits into a camera bag and could happily live on a bookshelf.

I’ve already photographed the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), the Pleiades (M45), the Dumbbell Nebula (M27) and the North America Nebula (NGC 7000). The results are excellent for such a small instrument, especially when imaging nebulas with its built-in dual-band filter, which helps reduce light pollution.

The Seestar app adds new in-app post-processing options, so you don’t have to mess around with any of that — though you can also export everything as lossless FITS files. The S30 Plus also includes a magnetic solar filter, enabling you to indulge in solar photography safely.

With Dwarflab’s $1,299 Draco (3.5-inch/90mm aperture) recently landed in stores and Vaonis’ own $4,990 Atlas (3.1-inch/80mm aperture) not available until 2027, ZWO’s decision to offer an upgraded entry-level smart telescope that buyers can get their hands on right now looks particularly smart.

With ZWO's pattern of delivering cheaper smart telescopes without sacrificing on quality, the Seestar S30 Plus could be one of Christmas 2026’s best gifts for anyone interested in astronomy — and maybe that’s the point of it. Either way, first impressions are good. A full review is coming tomorrow, so check back at Space.com to find out our full thoughts and testing.

#759. Why Quentin Tarantino Initially Fired Mélanie Laurent and Isabelle Huppert From ‘Inglourious Basterds’

"If it’s not right, it is not right. I don’t owe them sh**. I owe my film the best actors I can find. Period," the Oscar-winning filmmaker said in Jay Glennie’s new book.

Quentin Tarantino is getting candid about his decision to fire Mélanie Laurent and Isabelle Huppert before production began for 2009’s Inglourious Basterds.

The Oscar-winning filmmaker opened up in Jay Glennie’s new book, The Making of Quentin Tarantino’s Inglourious Basterds, about why he feels he doesn’t owe actors “shit,” but owes “my film the best actors I can find.”

The dark comedy war film, set in Nazi-occupied France during World War II, centers on a plan to assassinate Nazi leaders by a group of Jewish U.S. soldiers. However, the plan ends up coinciding with a theatre owner’s vengeful plans to do the same. Related Stories Exclusive Excerpt Brad Pitt, Tarantino and a Bong Full of Hash: The Untold Origin Story of 'Inglourious Basterds' Movies Cinemark Won't Screen Brad Pitt's 'Cliff Booth' Movie Over Netflix's Demands, CEO Says

Though Laurent was eventually rehired for the leading role of Shosanna Dreyfus, the French cinema owner, Tarantino said her initial “table read was terrible,” so he let her go.

“It wasn’t good enough to be terrible,” Tarantino told Glennie. “The most exciting day of preproduction is for me the table read. That is the closest I get to seeing the movie for the first time. Up until then, it’s just been me reading all the scenes to myself or to a friend … so a table read with the whole cast is so exciting and so important to me. Well, Mélanie was terrible, so I fired her.”

Tarantino recalled Laurent calling him to get her job back, explaining she was feeling under the weather at the time of the table read. A persistent Laurent also planned to show up to set regardless of his decision. “I will fly myself to Germany and put myself up into a hotel. I know you’re busy, but I will wait until you see me again,” she told the filmmaker.

She eventually convinced Tarantino to give her another chance, saying he would “turn the clock back” and “they would return to square one.” However, he wouldn’t fully decide if “she was his Shosanna Dreyfus” until after three days of rehearsal.

Laurent ultimately won over Tarantino, going on to play the lead role. “Let me just go on the record for everybody to know: I love Mélanie,” the director told the author.

“The fact of the matter is, if we were not talking about the making of Inglourious Basterds, I would never think about the table read again for the simple reason Mélanie is my Shosanna,” he added. “She did a wonderful job. But we have decided to dive deep into the making of the movie with this book, and this is an important part of its history. You know, we agreed, warts and all. So, if we had not agreed to talk about the shooting of the movie, it would be out of my mind, and I would never think about it again.”

Huppert was a bit of a different story. After being cast as Madame Ada Mimieux, a woman who provides shelter to Shosanna in Paris, Tarantino fired her when she didn’t show up for the table read.

“She didn’t show up, so fuck it. I fired her,” he said. “I mean, I love Isabelle Huppert — Heaven’s Gate and all that — but there were issues with her contract. It just kept stalling. And then not coming to the table read. Well, we cast Maggie Cheung instead.”

“That invariably happens. As far as I’m concerned, if you’re cast and you are not at that table, I don’t owe you jack shit! You can be fired, especially if I get excited by what somebody else did in your absence,” Tarantino continued. He used Michael Parks being cast in two different roles in his Kill Bill films, replacing Ricardo Montalbán, as another example.

Despite Cheung taking on the role, Tarantino ultimately decided to cut those scenes with her character from the movie.

“Maggie was fantastic in the movie, but you just didn’t need to know how Shosanna acquired the cinema. All we needed was a title card saying Four Years Later and Shosanna explaining that she inherited it from her aunt,” Tarantino explained.

Following its release in 2009, Inglourious Basterds went on to gross more than $321 million worldwide. It also earned eight Academy Award nominations, with Christoph Waltz taking home the best supporting actor Oscar for his role as Col. Hans Landa.

“I have no moral compass when it comes to giving roles to actors: They have to be right. They have to feel like they are right for the world I have created,” Tarantino told Glennie about his approach to casting actors. “I have fired actors in the past. If it’s not right, it is not right. I don’t owe them shit. I owe my film the best actors I can find. Period.”

#758. Scientists squeeze record-breaking X-ray power into an incredibly tiny spot

Scientists have achieved a new world record by producing extraordinarily intense X-ray flashes that last just 300 attoseconds, an almost unimaginably brief period of time. Using the European XFEL, a powerful X-ray research facility, the team concentrated the flashes into an area roughly 100,000 times smaller than the cross-section of a typical human hair.

By squeezing so much X-ray energy into such a tiny space, the researchers created an exceptionally powerful beam that could open new possibilities for studying the behavior of electrons inside atoms and molecules. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists observe the rapid movements of electrons during chemical reactions and potentially even learn to control them.

The experiment took place in April 2026, and the findings have now been published in the scientific journal Optica.

Record-Breaking X-Ray Flashes Last Just 300 Attoseconds

"This is a world record in intensity and fluence for a hard-X-ray attosecond pulse," says Ichiro Inoue from the University of Tokyo, first author of the publication.

Hard X-rays are a form of light with extremely short wavelengths. Scientists use two measurements to describe their extraordinary power. Fluence refers to the amount of energy delivered to a particular area, while intensity also considers how quickly that energy is delivered.

In this experiment, each X-ray pulse lasted an estimated 300 attoseconds (an attosecond is a billionth of a billionth of a second). Such incredibly short flashes offer researchers a way to investigate events that unfold far too quickly for conventional observation.

To concentrate the X-rays, the team used a specialized optical arrangement called an advanced Kirkpatrick-Baez, or AKB, system. It consists of two exceptionally precise mirrors that focus the beam in different directions. Each pulse underwent four reflections in total, with one mirror focusing the X-rays vertically and the other horizontally.

The result was an astonishingly small focal spot measuring just 180 × 330 nanometers (a nanometre is a billionth of a meter). By directing the energy into this microscopic area, the researchers were able to achieve record-breaking intensity.

"A few years ago, we demonstrated terawatt-scale hard X-ray attosecond pulses at the European XFEL," says DESY scientist Jiawei Yan, one of the corresponding authors of the study. "But generating powerful pulses is only the first step. For experiments, what really matters is what we can deliver to the sample. With this advance, we can now use attosecond X-rays to explore highly nonlinear interactions between X-rays and matter."

These nonlinear interactions occur when extremely intense X-rays cause matter to respond in ways that would not normally happen under weaker illumination. Studying such effects could reveal new details about how atoms and electrons behave under extreme conditions.

An Extraordinary Reaction Inside Copper Atoms

To confirm the exceptional intensity of their X-ray pulses, the researchers directed them at a thin sheet of copper. The experiment provided independent evidence that the focused flashes reached peak intensities exceeding 10²⁰ watts per square centimeter.

When the X-rays struck the copper, they knocked electrons out of the atoms' innermost electron shells, leaving behind empty positions known as 'holes'. Electrons from other parts of the atoms then moved into these vacancies, releasing energy in the form of X-ray light.

Under ordinary circumstances, this emitted light travels in many different directions. However, when the incoming X-rays become sufficiently intense, something remarkable happens. The emitted light can stimulate other excited copper atoms to release additional X-rays traveling in the same direction, producing an amplified beam.

Scientists call this phenomenon amplified spontaneous emission, or ASE.

"It is almost magical to see this happening," says Anders Madsen, group leader at the MID instrument, where the study was conducted. "Normal fluorescence goes in all directions, regardless of the direction of the incoming beam. But when the ASE threshold is crossed, you see the light cone starting to condense into the forward direction."

The team also observed another important signature of extreme intensity. As they increased the energy of the X-ray pulses, the amplified signal initially became much stronger. At higher energies, however, the increase slowed and eventually leveled off, a behavior known as saturation.

This pattern is expected only under exceptionally intense X-ray illumination. Its appearance provided additional confirmation of the record intensity calculated from the pulse energy, duration, and size of the focused beam.

A New Way to Explore the Hidden World of Electrons

Beyond setting a world record, the breakthrough could significantly expand scientists' ability to investigate some of nature's fastest processes.

Electrons play a central role in determining how atoms bond together, how molecules interact, and how chemical reactions unfold. Their movements happen on extraordinarily short timescales, making them difficult to observe directly.

By combining ultrashort X-ray flashes with extremely high intensity, researchers hope to capture information about electrons before the incoming radiation has time to substantially alter the material being studied. This could provide a clearer picture of electron behavior inside atoms and molecules and, in the longer term, potentially lead to methods for influencing electron motion during chemical reactions.

The advanced Kirkpatrick-Baez mirror system used for the record-setting experiment was transported from Japan. European XFEL is now preparing to receive its own AKB system, with delivery expected in early 2027.

The new equipment is being funded through a collaboration with the University of Hamburg, with additional support from the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space (BMFTR).

Once the system has been installed and commissioned, scientists from around the world using the MID instrument are expected to gain access to these exceptionally brief and intense X-ray flashes. The upgraded capabilities could allow researchers to investigate electron behavior at a level of detail that has previously been difficult to achieve, bringing them closer to understanding and potentially controlling the fundamental processes behind chemical reactions.

#757. ‘SVU’ Star Mariska Hargitay Breaks Down Benson and Stabler’s Complicated Reunion and Her Final Choice: ‘There Are So Many Feelings’

SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers from the 600th episode of “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit.”

To say that Olivia Benson and Elliot Stabler have a complicated relationship would be an understatement. During the Nov. 12 600th episode of “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit,” Benson (Mariska Hargitay) is forced to reopen a case that she worked with Stabler (Christopher Meloni) many years ago, realizing they likely put the wrong man behind bars. Related Stories Oscar Predictions: Best Casting — 'Being Heumann' and 'La Bola Negra' Found the Year's Boldest Discoveries. Will the Academy Reward Them? Florence Pugh Says 'I'm Not Standing for Bulls--- Behavior' on Set Anymore: 'Show Up on Time, Don’t Be Rude, Don’t Be a Misogynist'

After convincing him to come help her with the case, Benson learns that he had shut her out of the case and taken control, something she allowed him to do. But she’s the captain now — and isn’t going to allow their old patterns to return.

“I love that we got to push up against each other because that’s also family. There are so many feelings between Benson and Stabler. It’s so complicated — what could have been, what was, what we’ve shared, the ‘ride or die,'” says Hargitay. “People ask, ‘Why do you think people love Benson and Stabler?’ And it’s because of their dedication to each other, their trust in each other.”

Since Stabler “was so formative in her development as a detective,” this episode highlighted how they move past that. “It’s about a woman having her voice,” she says. “So many women identify with that.”

Hargitay was excited to dive into such a strong storyline about the duo.

“I think that we also just wanted to tell a truthful, complex story that people could identify with, have big feelings about, and understand the complexities of these types of relationships, and give them something real to go up against,” she adds. “We are so focused on keeping it real and making it good, and we know that just by being together, the fans will be happy. That’s why we invited him back because we knew they’d be so happy, and that’s what they would want. But also, he’s such a big part of the story. It’s truthful to have him back at this juncture.”

At the end of the episode, Stabler invites Benson to take some time off and go away for a few days. The audience knows she has days off available, since it’s specifically mentioned early on, but that doesn’t mean she says yes. In fact, it was never even an option, says Hargitay.

“No. There are a lot of reasons why not,” she says. “It’s not where they are now — either one of them.”

NASA's Curiosity Mars rover is sizing up its next dig site on the Red Planet.

The Curiosity team will characterize the surface composition of the Mars site, informally named "Nazca," as thoroughly as possible before drilling into it.

Curiosity snapped the close-up image on Oct. 18, 2026, using its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI). The image shows multiple roughly disk-shaped potential crystal formations at the rover's next drill target.

MAHLI is located on the turret at the end of the rover's robotic arm. It uses an onboard focusing process to make a composite of images of the same target acquired at different positions to focus on multiple features in a single image.

Scientists theorize that the "discs and needles" texture takes its characteristic shape as crystals, or "crystal forms," grow.

The relatively large sizes of the crystal forms at "Nazca" may provide clues about the temperatures at which they grew, as well as information about the abundance of salts and fluids in the area at the time. Complicating this picture, however, is the fact that mineral crystals can be replaced by other minerals after their original crystallization. The new minerals are known as "pseudomorphs," because they have the same shape as the original minerals but not the same composition or molecular structure.

The Curiosity team will characterize the surface composition of Nazca — which shares its name with an ancient South American civilization that's famous for the large designs it etched into the rock and dirt — before drilling begins. The NASA researchers will then be able to compare the deeper composition to the surface-level composition.

#755. Massive atlas of brain region linked to a host of diseases is the most detailed yet

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Miryam Naddaf is a reporter for Nature in London.

The basal ganglia are groups of cells that sit deep in the brain and process motor, cognitive, mood and decision-making information. They are linked to neurodegenerative and psychiatric conditions from Parkinson’s and Huntington’s disease to schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and addiction.

Now, researchers have published the world’s most-detailed atlas of basal ganglia so far, comprising 25.5 million brain cells from humans, macaques and marmosets. The work is described in a collection of 26 papers published in Cell, Cell Reports, Cell Reports Methods, Cell Systems, Cell Genomics and Neuron. The research includes understudied neurons1, provides insights about how some brain cells change with age2 and suggests which might be linked to diseases3.

The atlas, a collaboration between hundreds of scientists in nine countries, is part of the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) — a US$500-million project launched in 2022 by the US National Institutes of Health aimed at creating reference maps of mammalian brains.

“It’s a massive dictionary that we needed in the field,” says Ana Muñoz-Manchado, a neuroscientist at the University of Cádiz in Spain, who studies the basal ganglia in neurodegenerative disorders.

The basal ganglia atlas contains 21 million cells from the brains of six humans, three million cells from three rhesus and cynomolgus macaques, and 1.5 million cells from two marmosets4. The researchers also used data from previously published maps of the whole mouse brain5,6.

By comparing the basal ganglia between the primate species, the researchers identified 61 cell types in humans, macaques and marmosets that have been conserved over 76 million years3.

The team analysed brain tissue samples from different developmental stages across the lifespan of the species. The latest work combines information about these cells in unprecedented detail, from measurements of their gene expression and DNA modifications that control gene regulation to recordings of their electrical activity, as well as how DNA is folded inside their nuclei.

The researchers also mapped where each cell is located in the brain and designed a common framework to characterize and annotate the cells. It is “essentially a scaffold on which we can now fairly readily complete the rest of the brain”, explains Michael Hawrylycz, a bioinformatician at the Allen Institute for Brain Science in Seattle, Washington, who took part in the project.

One study examined 1.1 million cells in the basal ganglia’s largest structure — known as the striatum — from 19 deceased human donors7. Unlike many other brain areas, the striatum has no neat anatomical boundaries. The researchers identified six zones in the human and macaque striatum with distinct molecular signatures, each containing distinct populations of neurons and glial cells.

“The cells in these zones all look the same under the microscope, but have very strong transcriptional differences and are strikingly consistent from person to person,” said co-author Evan Macosko, a neurobiologist at the Broad Institute of Harvard and MIT in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in a press release from the institute.

Macosko and his colleagues also found that gene expression patterns that distinguished each zone from the other became increasingly similar with age, particularly in brain regions affected by Huntington’s and Parkinson’s disease.

Another study analysed nearly four million cells in the striatum and prefrontal cortex from 178 deceased adult donors between the ages of 27 and over 902. The researchers found that the cellular make-up of the two brain regions varied between people, particularly for non-neuronal cells known as glial cells. This underscores the need for brain cell atlases to account for these individual differences.

#754. ‘Law & Order: SVU’ Goes Back to (Before) the Beginning With Its 600th Episode

Showrunner Michele Fazekas breaks down Christopher Meloni's return and the state of the Benson-Stabler relationship.

[This story contains spoilers from the 600th episode of Law & Order: SVU.]

Law & Order: SVU reached a huge milestone Thursday: 600 episodes, a number that only two scripted primetime shows have ever hit before. The cast and crew celebrated with a cake on set during filming and a dinner afterward — and then went back to work. Six hundred episodes is an extremely rare feat for a scripted series (The Simpsons and Gunsmoke are the only ones with more), but Thursday’s episode was also the sixth of season 28; 15 more are still to come. Related Stories Business Fanatics Studios' Next Big Media Play Is the NBA All-Star Game TV Jason Benetti Will Replace Dan Hicks on Notre Dame Play-by-Play Saturday Following Sudden Passing (Exclusive)

“That’s just doing television,” showrunner Michele Fazekas told The Hollywood Reporter. “It’s our 600th episode, but it’s also just an episode within 21 episodes [this season]. You’re working on five episodes at the same time at any given moment — you’re in prep on some episodes, you’re writing on some episodes, you’re in post on some episodes. Nothing changed in that regard.”

Titled “Obedience,” the 600th episode brings Elliot Stabler (Christopher Meloni) back to the Special Victims Unit after jury consultant Gwen Sharpe (J. Smith-Cameron, who also appeared in the season premiere) convinces Benson (Mariska Hargitay) to take another look at an old case. Gwen is convinced the man in prison for the crime, the rape and murder of a young nun in 1998, is innocent.

Stabler is reluctant to revisit the case — with good reason, it turns out. He failed to follow a couple of leads that could have pointed to the real culprit, a now-retired priest who led mass at the convent where the victim lived. He also cut Benson out of the interrogation in the case, which she went along with at the time because she was new to the squad. The case stirs up complicated feelings in the former partners; when Stabler asks Benson why she’s so interested in digging up the case, she retorts, “Why aren’t you?”

He eventually agrees to work with her, and the pair head upstate to question people who knew the victim (most notably, guest stars Laura Innes and Kathleen Chalfant) and track down the priest.

Fazekas, who wrote the episode (Brenna Malloy directed), said she wanted to give the 600th show the feel of “an old school Benson and Stabler episode” while also looking at the people they have become in the years since. To that end, the episode’s final scenes will give viewers plenty to discuss.

Fazekas unpacked those scenes, the reasons for going back to the show’s early days and more in an interview with THR.

Given the milestone that this is, was there extra planning that went into it? Or did you have ideas on the board for longer than you might normally?

Probably a little bit. I think I had an idea early on in the in the season of what I wished to do, and one of the first things was saying, “Can we bring back Chris Meloni?” Assuming that this is the last centennial episode that we were going to have, it feels like if we could do it, this would be the time to do it. So yeah, there were some earlier ideas than your typical running around trying to figure out what an episode is.

Having Stabler come back into the squad was always part of the plan, then?

It was for me. There were a lot of things that had to happen in order for that to become a reality, including Chris having to be available — he’s busy. But he was. I also knew early on — because I was on the show the first time around, seasons three through seven — I wanted to kind of go back a little bit to an old school Benson and Stabler episode of SVU and honor that era of the show. I just had an idea, and I don’t usually come up with ideas this way, but I was like, “I want it to be a road show.” I want them to be in a car, driving long distances and hashing stuff out. I didn’t know what [the reason] was. I always find that interesting, just putting two people in a place where they can’t get away, and then they have to hash out their stuff.

The structure of SVU is such that cases usually get cleared and some sort of justice is served by the end of the hour. I thought it was really interesting that this one is built on something that they got wrong initially. Why did you want to come at it that way?

In part, it was because you have to explain why are we bringing Detective Stabler back. He doesn’t work in SVU anymore. He works in a completely different department. So what would be big enough that he would come back? It felt sort of organic for it to be an old case, but it’s a case that actually predates the show. The show starts in 1999, and this case is from 1998.

What was not planned but came out in the in the breaking of the story is they were such different people back then. Benson was really new, and Stabler was the senior detective, and she has evolved so much because, at the end of the day, we’re still telling the story of Benson. It fits really nicely into what we’re doing with her character this season, and it made sense for why he’s back. But it also goes to wanting to do and old school SVU episodes, but let’s go back to before SVU was even a thing.

I was also struck by Stabler admitting to Benson that his Catholicism might have blinded him to who the real perpetrator was. His religion has been a thread throughout the character’s run, but I think it’s always interesting when it comes up explicitly in relation to a case.

Chris Meloni was a big proponent of that as well. I think allowing your own preconceptions biases you; it goes to that whole issue [of blind spots] generally. Anybody who was raised Catholic, you think of it as one thing, and it’s very hard for people to accept that this thing that you think is one way has a really dark side. At that time [in 1998], it would have been really hard for Stabler to even understand.

You were on the show for a good portion of the Benson-Stabler partnership during your first tenure, and now you’re back as showrunner. What’s your read on their relationship?

My read is Stabler still has work to do on himself that Benson has done. Benson has evolved in a way, and I love them together, and I love them as partners and as scene partners. But I think part of this episode is talking about how she, in some ways, has moved on from the struggles back then. I think Stabler is still working on it. Stabler is still doing a lot of the same things that he did 20 years ago, and he’s starting to realize, oh, I need to change that.

And given what goes on between them in this episode — arguing about work and life, and then him inviting her to come to Arizona for a while — what do you think the audience’s read is going to be?

Listen, I do think they love each other. I think they both know. I think when he says, “Hey, you want to come to Arizona?” he knows her answer is going to be no. It’s easy to ask that question when you know the answer is no. I don’t think he didn’t mean it, but he also knew what her answer was going to be, and I think now is not the time. Is there time down the line? Maybe, but I think he’s got some work to do. She can have some work to do as well, but I think she’s probably a little further down that path than he is.

I’ve always thought that they love each other in a way that sort of transcends a sexual relationship. They deeply love each other, and they’ve acknowledged that before, and I think this sort of reinforces it. But I also think he knows I’ve got more to do with myself.

Where are you in terms of production now?

We are shooting episode 10 and in prep on episode 11.

Anything you can say about the next few episodes?

We have a nice little arc going of that we started at the beginning of the season that we continue, where the cases that they’re faced with are messy and don’t have easy answers. Benson is really struggling with feeling like nothing has changed. No matter how hard we work, sometimes it doesn’t matter. I like the idea of pushing her — the episode we’re shooting now and the next episode are pushing her to the edges of not even what is legal, but what is ethically and morally right to do, because she’s starting to not care.

The episode we’re shooting right now, the bad guy is so bad. We’re talking about “Why is he doing what he’s doing?” And she actually says, “I don’t care,” which is a big thing for her. But you also understand it because the guy is such a bad guy.

Anything you can say about how Stephanie March re-enters the show as Alex Cabot?

Benson goes to her and asks for help. They didn’t end things on a totally happy note the last time she was on the show, but Benson goes back to her.

Is Alex still doing the same sort of work she was that last time?

#753. Scientists discover Europe's ancient forests were nothing like we imagined

Picture the wilderness of central Europe 100,000 years ago, or even a million years ago. You might imagine an endless expanse of towering trees, with thick canopies blocking sunlight from reaching the ground. But according to a major new study, that familiar image of Europe's ancient forests is probably misleading.

Instead, much of the continent was a vibrant landscape of scattered trees, open woodlands, grassy clearings, and colorful wildflower meadows. Birds and butterflies flourished in these sunlit habitats, while enormous grazing animals helped prevent trees and shrubs from taking over.

Researchers led by Aarhus University have found that this mixture of habitats dominated Europe's landscapes for more than 20 million years. Far from being the continent's original natural condition, the dense, dark forests common in many parts of Europe today appear to be a relatively recent development in its ecological history.

Published in Biological Conservation, the findings challenge a longstanding assumption about what Europe's wilderness looked like before widespread human intervention. They also raise important questions about modern reforestation programs, which often prioritize planting dense forests to combat climate change and protect biodiversity.

"The study shows that current reforestation practices are on the wrong track - both here in Denmark, where subsidies are only granted for planting dense forests, and elsewhere in Europe. This will not only be harmful for biodiversity; it will be in direct contradiction to the type of ecosystems that Europe's species have evolved in over millions of years," says Professor Jens-Christian Svenning from the Center for Ecological Dynamics in a Novel Biosphere (ECONOVO), Department of Biology at Aarhus University, senior author of the study.

Challenging the Myth of Europe's Ancient Forests

For decades, conservation strategies have been influenced by the "closed-forest paradigm." This is the belief that dense forests with nearly continuous tree canopies were Europe's natural landscape before humans began clearing land for agriculture and settlements.

Under this view, restoring nature often means allowing trees to reclaim open areas or planting forests where they no longer exist.

The new research suggests that this approach may overlook a crucial part of Europe's ecological history. Rather than being uniformly covered by dense forests, the continent was characterized by changing combinations of grasslands, shrubs, and woodlands with different amounts of tree cover.

These landscapes supported a rich variety of species adapted to both wooded and open environments. Large plant-eating animals also played a major role in maintaining this diversity by grazing, browsing, and disturbing vegetation.

What 23 Million Years of Evidence Reveals

To reconstruct Europe's ancient environments, the researchers examined an unusually extensive collection of evidence spanning millions of years.

Previous studies have generally concentrated on more recent periods. This investigation extended much further into the past, examining paleoecological records from the Miocene epoch (which began around 23 million years ago) through the pre-industrial era.

Paleoecology is the study of ancient ecosystems using clues preserved in fossils, sediments, and other natural records. Because no single type of evidence can provide a complete picture of the distant past, the team combined several independent methods.

These included fossilized pollen and larger plant remains, charcoal left by ancient wildfires, and chemical signatures preserved in the teeth and bones of plant-eating animals. The researchers also examined fossil insects and mammals, along with ancient environmental DNA recovered from sediments.

Environmental DNA consists of genetic material left behind by organisms in their surroundings. When preserved in ancient deposits, it can help scientists identify plants and animals that lived in an area long ago.

Together, these different sources of evidence allowed the researchers to reconstruct not only what types of vegetation existed, but also how ecosystems changed over time and how animals influenced their surroundings.

"Each type of proxy offers its own perspective, but together they let us see whether the landscapes were covered by dense forests, open grasslands, or a mix of the two. By combining these datasets across time - from the Miocene to the pre-industrial era - we could trace long-term changes in vegetation and the role of large herbivores with much greater confidence than earlier studies that used only one method," explains the study's lead author, ECONOVO PhD student Szymon Czyzewski of Aarhus University.

The evidence points to a consistent pattern. Across more than 20 million years, Europe's landscapes were typically a shifting mosaic of trees, open spaces, and flowering plants rather than continuous stretches of closed forest.

Importantly, these mixed landscapes were not limited to one particular climate. They existed under temperate conditions comparable to those in much of Europe today, as well as during warmer and colder periods.

Elephants, Rhinos, and Bison Shaped Europe's Wilderness

One of the most striking findings concerns the influence of large wild herbivores.

Ancient Europe was home to animals such as elephants, rhinoceroses, aurochs, and bison. By feeding on vegetation and disturbing the ground as they moved, these animals helped keep parts of the landscape open.

Their activities created opportunities for grasses, wildflowers, and other plants that might otherwise have struggled beneath dense tree cover.

This constant interaction between animals and vegetation helped sustain a diverse mixture of habitats, providing suitable conditions for many different species.

Modern Europe, however, is missing much of this ecological influence. Many of the large wild herbivores that once shaped its landscapes have disappeared, and traditional grazing practices have also declined.

"The ecosystems we see in Europe today lack the large wild herbivores that not only shaped landscapes but also sustained its biodiversity for millions of years. The most dramatic shift has largely taken place within the last hundred years, when traditional extensive grazing disappeared from large parts of the landscape," says Czyzewski.

This loss of grazing pressure has changed how vegetation develops across much of the continent, helping explain why present-day European ecosystems differ so dramatically from those of the distant past.

Europe's Ancient Woodlands Were Full of Wildflowers

The research also offers a different perspective on species commonly associated with farmland and other human-managed environments.

Birds such as larks and jackdaws, along with mammals such as the European hamster, are often regarded as characteristic of agricultural landscapes. Yet the researchers suggest that their evolutionary histories likely extend back to the open woodland environments that existed long before modern farming.

Even familiar wildflowers have connections to these ancient ecosystems.

Wild poppies, now frequently seen growing in agricultural fields, also thrived in areas where large grazing animals disturbed vegetation within ancient woodlands.

These findings challenge the sharp distinction between "forest" and "open habitats" that often guides conservation planning today.

In Europe's ecological past, trees, meadows, shrubs, and grazing animals were not necessarily separate parts of nature. They frequently existed together, forming interconnected habitats that supported a wide range of wildlife.

Why Planting More Trees May Not Always Help Nature

The findings arrive as European countries continue expanding forests to capture carbon dioxide, address climate change, and restore biodiversity.

Although forests can provide important environmental benefits, the researchers argue that planting large areas of uniformly dense woodland may not be the best approach when the goal is to restore Europe's native ecosystems.

Many European species evolved in landscapes containing a mixture of trees and open areas. Converting these habitats into continuous closed-canopy forests could therefore reduce the variety of environments available to wildlife.

The study suggests that restoration efforts should focus more strongly on maintaining diverse landscapes, including open grasslands, scattered woodland, and areas shaped by natural grazing.

"Instead, restoration efforts should place greater emphasis on creating and maintaining mosaics of woodland and open habitats - not least through the restoration of natural-living large herbivores," Svenning concludes.

The findings add to a growing body of research from the same scientific group suggesting that large animals played a far greater role in shaping Europe's ecosystems than previously recognized.

They also reinforce the idea that Europe's ancient landscapes were generally brighter, more open, and more varied than the dense primeval forests often depicted in popular imagination.

Rather than restoring nature by simply planting more trees, the researchers suggest that protecting biodiversity may require recreating the complex balance of woodlands, meadows, and grazing animals that shaped the continent for millions of years.

The familiar image of Europe as a vast, dark, unbroken forest may be deeply rooted in our understanding of nature, but millions of years of evidence are painting a very different picture.

A robot just played Tinkertoys in space, assembling the first satellite structure ever made without a human touching the controls.

The DARPA-funded project saw a robotic "truss builder" create a reflective antenna using Kapton film, composite fiber tubes and aluminum joints. The implications are huge for future missions, potentially opening up new possibilities to build — or fix — satellites in the final frontier.

"This is the first time that a structure has been autonomously constructed in space," Sergio Pellegrino, an aerospace and civil engineering professor at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement on Nov. 5.

The need for such spacecraft will likely rise substantially in the future, as companies assemble giant megaconstellations for cell-phone communications, AI compute and other purposes. Indeed, the ball is already rolling on such ambitious projects, generating enough hype for space startups around the globe to raise a record $20.8 billion in the third quarter of 2026 alone.

Anything that launches aboard a rocket is limited by the size of that vehicle's fairing — the nose cone that protects payloads during their ride to space. In space, however, the ability to stretch out is practically infinite — after taking into account, of course, engineering and financing constraints.

Assembling structures robotically off Earth could therefore be revolutionary, advocates say. And the recent milestone was a step in that direction.

"This work could be useful not only for astronomy and astrophysics, but also for communications and other areas, such as building very large solar arrays for space solar power," said Pellegrino, who's team leader of the truss-building project, a Caltech demonstration mission called Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly (ASTRA).

ASTRA built a 1.4-meter-wide (4.5-foot) structure in orbit. That's an impressive achievement, but it just scratches the surface of what DARPA wants to accomplish via a program it calls Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-efficient Design, or NOM4D for short.

"NOM4D's objective is to enable efficient, scalable construction of very large structures in space," NOM4D Program Manager Andrew Detor said in a Nov. 5 DARPA statement.

"By 'very large,' I mean hundreds of meters or kilometers in scale. Nothing approaching that scale can be achieved today," Detor added.

ASTRA was a demonstration, allowing researchers to check boxes and identify obstacles before shooting for a bigger goal. And the team did run into issues — specifically, time limitations, which prevented them from building additional sections of the antenna. Still, the researchers were able to prove out the third phase of a larger DARPA project.

Pellegrino's team completed the two previous phases — defining the mission and testing the hardware in a lab — before shipping the ASTRA payload to the spaceflight company Momentus, Inc. for integration into its Vigoride 7 space tug. Vigoride 7 launched on March 30, along with many other payloads, aboard SpaceX's Transporter-16 rideshare mission.

ASTRA flew with two prebuilt sections of a truss, a robotic "manipulator" and parts to make the rest of the truss in space. In brief communication windows totaling 15 minutes a day, engineers sent up commands and checked in on the robot's progress as it picked up things, readied them in the right spot, and performed construction on an assembly plate.

The team overcame many "little surprises" on the way but were not able to finish the entire truss in time. Still, Pellegrino framed the effort as a success.

"Developing a payload of this complexity on such a short timeline was an enormous undertaking for our small team," he said.

Looking into the future, he is hopeful that robots will be able to build larger telescope mirrors for observatories to peer deeper into space, as well as more advanced structures for radio telescopes to listen for distant signals.

NOM4D is also supporting a project from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, but that one will take place at the International Space Station, focusing on how to harden carbon tubes in orbit.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#750. Latin Grammys 2026: Rosalía Wins Album of the Year

Janet Jackson also presented Daddy Yankee with the person of the year honor.

Spanish singer Rosalía took home the top prize of album of the year at the 2026 Latin Grammys on Thursday night for her 2025 album Lux.

She opened the 27th annual Latin Grammy Awards, live from Sin City, with an emotive medley of her Lux tracks “La Rumba Del Perdón,” “La Perla” and “Dios Es Un Stalker,” joined by angelic dancers ornamented with halos atop a stage meant to look like heavenly clouds.

It was a reminder of the expansiveness of her album: an offbeat, full-hearted embrace of her classical training through huge orchestral movements, inspired by the lives of female saints. Related Stories TV How to Stream the 2026 Latin Grammys Online Movies 'Wet,' Starring Connor Storrie, Rebecca Ferguson and Odessa A'zion, Acquired by Lionsgate

Her “La Perla” also won song of the year, and during her speech, she thanked Mexico and invited her collaborators on the song, the American urban sierreño trio Yahritza Y Su Esencia, to join her on stage.

Daddy Yankee, the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards’ person of the year and first Latin urbano artist to receive the honor, ripped through his biggest hits an hour into Thursday’s award show, treating the stage like a stadium floor.

It was one for the history books: There were outfit changes, set changes and his native Puerto Rico always at the forefront as he ran through “Ella Me Levantó,” “Con Calma,” “BOTZ,” “Despacito,” “Lo Que Pasó, Pasó,” “Sonríele,” “Rompe,” “Pokito” and, of course, “Gasolina” — joined by Bizarrap, Bad Gyal, Feid, Jay Wheeler, French Montana, LL Cool J and Diljit Dosanjh.

When it came time for Daddy Yankee to receive his honor, it was delivered to him by Janet Jackson “with admiration and respect,” as she said in her speech. When he accepted the award, he concluded by saying “Puerto Rico, recuerda. … Puerto Rico no es pequeño. Pequeño el mapa.” In English: “Puerto Rico, remember. … Puerto Rico is not small. The map is small.”

The award show took place live from Las Vegas’ MGM Grand Garden Arena. It aired live on Univision, UniMás, Galavisión and ViX and hosted by actor, producer and musician Roselyn Sánchez.

For the first award of the night, Pablo Alboran and Backstreet Boys’ Howie D presented Juanes with best pop/rock album for Juanesteban.

Performances were at a high level: Karol G was joined by a full orchestra and 12 Mariachis for her música mexicana ballad “Ese Hombre es Malo.” Mon Laferte broke hearts with her soulful “Femme Fatale.” Silvana Estrada’s “Dime” bridged culture and heritage with her signature Venezuelan cuatro, a four-stringed instrument similar in structure to a ukulele.

Kany García stunned with her acoustic, aflamencado single “La Niña Que Fui.” The Uruguayan-born Jorge Drexler’s rendition of “Las Palabras” felt like theater. And Argentine rapper Milo J performed “Solifican12” and “Gil,” joined by the Latin American folk icon Gustavo Santaolalla.

Carín León brought the house down with “Desde Que Te Tengo,” as did Juanes and Vivir Quintana with “Humano.” Elena Rose was joined by sword-wielding dancers for “Alma.”

Brazilian superstar Anitta did a medley of her “Equilibrium” hits — “Desgraça,” “Choka Choka” and “Meia Noite” among them — an eclectic mix of Brazilian funk, samba, bossa nova, semba, reggae, electronic pop performed in Portuguese, Spanish and English.

Soon after, she was back on stage accepting the trophy for Portuguese language contemporary pop album. She used her speech to shine a light on the Black culture of her native Brazil.

There was a touching tribute to the late ranchera icon, Mexican singer-songwriter José Alfredo Jiménez, produced by Edgar Barrera: The Warning covered “Te Solté la Rienda,” Reik did “La Media Vuelta,” Sofía Reyes and Yami Safdie dueted “Si Nos Dejan” and Camila Fernández brought it home with a big belting “El Rey.” Not soon afterward, she headed back to the stage to perform a full-throated “Serpiente De Cascabel.”

It was the first of two tributes: The second was for Willie Colón, the social activist and Grammy-nominated architect of urban salsa music, who died in February of this year. His son, Miguel Colón, as well as Nathy Peluso and Luis Figueroa and others performed.

Awards were handed out quickly, too. Karol G took home the trophy for urban music album for Tropicoqueta. Xavi won contemporary Mexican album for Dosis, his first Latin Grammy. Fonseca was presented the trophy for contemporary tropical album shortly thereafter for his album, Antes Que El Tiempo Se Vaya.

Best new artist went to Colombian singer Aria Vega, who gave her acceptance speech through tears. This year, the Latin Recording Academy made changes to the category so that only artists with fewer than three albums or 25 singles released were eligible to win.

Most of the evening’s awards were handed out during a pre-televised Premiere Ceremony. That included Bobby Pulido winning the Latin Grammy for best Tejano album for his release Bobby Pulido & Friends: Una Tuya y Una Mía (Vol. 2/En Vivo). Just days earlier, Pulido made history in the U.S. midterm elections by securing a seat in the House of Representatives for the Democrats by flipping a Texas district seat.

“I want to tell you that I’m retiring from music, and I’m leaving with so much gratitude,” he said in his acceptance speech.

#749. Scientists wipe out deadly brain tumors in every mouse tested with new cancer therapy

Scientists at UC San Francisco have developed a new type of immune cell therapy that activates only after entering the brain, allowing it to attack cancer while remaining inactive elsewhere in the body.

In experiments involving mice, the engineered cells successfully eliminated diffuse midline glioma (DMG), an aggressive childhood brain cancer that spreads into surrounding healthy tissue. The treatment also provided lasting protection. When researchers introduced cancer cells again several weeks later, the immune cells continued fighting and prevented new tumors from developing.

DMG is among the most difficult childhood cancers to treat. It grows into the brainstem, a critical region that regulates breathing, heartbeat, and swallowing. Nearly all children diagnosed with the disease die within a year, and existing treatments have had little success in stopping its progression.

The experimental therapy, called B-SYNC CAR-T, could offer a new way forward. Unlike conventional CAR-T treatments, which have struggled against brain tumors, these modified immune cells are programmed to activate their cancer-fighting machinery specifically within the brain. Researchers suspect this targeted approach makes the cells more effective, although the precise reason remains unclear.

The promising results have prompted scientists to prepare for clinical trials at UCSF Health, potentially beginning as early as April 2027.

"It's been a struggle to make CAR-T cells that overcome DMG without causing unacceptable side effects," said Hideho Okada, MD, PhD, a professor of Neurological Surgery at UCSF and co-corresponding author of the study, published October 28 in Science Translational Medicine. "By limiting B-SYNC's CAR expression to when and where it matters -- in the brain -- we saw consistent, total shutdown of DMG tumors in the lab."

Engineering Smarter CAR-T Cells to Fight Brain Cancer

B-SYNC builds on years of research by Okada and Wendell Lim, PhD, a professor of Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology at UCSF. Their goal has been to develop immune cells that can recognize and destroy brain tumors with greater precision.

CAR-T therapy works by modifying the body's T cells, a type of immune cell, so they carry special receptors called CARs. These receptors recognize proteins on cancer cells and trigger an immune attack. Although CAR-T treatments have shown success against certain cancers, brain tumors have remained particularly difficult to overcome.

In 2021, Okada and Lim reported encouraging laboratory findings with an earlier therapy called E-SYNC, designed to treat glioblastoma, another aggressive form of brain cancer.

E-SYNC uses a molecular sensing system known as synNotch to identify EGFRvIII, a mutated protein found on some glioblastoma cells. When this protein is detected, synNotch directs the immune cell to produce a CAR that recognizes two additional tumor-associated proteins, EphA2 and IL13Rα2. This two-step process proved more effective than conventional CAR-T strategies that rely on a single activation step.

However, the approach had an important limitation. Only about 20% of patients have tumors containing EGFRvIII. Even when the protein is initially present, tumors can lose it as treatment eliminates the cancer cells carrying it. This allows remaining cancer cells to escape detection.

To overcome that problem, the researchers searched for a more dependable signal that could activate the therapy in a wider range of patients.

A Molecular Switch That Activates Inside the Brain

The scientists identified brevican, a protein naturally distributed throughout the brain, as a promising alternative.

They redesigned the synNotch system so that it would trigger CAR production only when it encountered brevican. Once activated, these "B-SYNC" CAR-T cells could search for cancer cells carrying EphA2 or IL13Rα2, even if those cells lacked EGFRvIII.

This meant the engineered immune cells no longer depended on a tumor-specific mutation to become active. Instead, they used a protein associated with the brain itself as the signal to begin their attack.

Although B-SYNC was initially developed for glioblastoma, the researchers recognized that it might also work against DMG. Both cancers commonly display EphA2 and IL13Rα2 on their tumor cells, making them potential targets for the same treatment.

Senthilnath Lakshmanachetty, PhD, a postdoctoral researcher in Okada's laboratory, led experiments to investigate whether B-SYNC could successfully attack this deadly childhood cancer.

New CAR-T Therapy Eliminates Brain Tumors in Mice

The researchers first administered B-SYNC CAR-T cells intravenously (IV) to mice implanted with human DMG cells.

Some of the engineered immune cells traveled through the bloodstream and entered the brain. Once there, they began producing the cancer-targeting CAR receptors and attacking tumor cells.

Importantly, this activation appeared to occur only in the intended location. B-SYNC cells elsewhere in the body, including those circulating in the blood or present in the spleen, did not produce the CAR receptors.

That was "just as we designed it," Lakshmanachetty said.

The team next examined whether delivering the treatment directly into the brain would produce stronger results. They administered B-SYNC using an intracerebroventricular (ICV) injection, which introduces the cells into the brain's fluid-filled ventricles.

The results were striking. In two mouse models containing human DMG tumors, the treatment completely eliminated the cancer in every mouse tested. Conventional CAR-T cells, by comparison, were unable to bring the tumors under control.

The findings suggested that activating the engineered immune cells specifically within the brain could overcome some of the obstacles that have limited earlier CAR-T treatments.

Immune Cells Keep Fighting Long After Tumors Disappear

Destroying the original tumors was only part of the achievement. The researchers also wanted to determine whether the engineered immune cells could remain active and protect against cancer returning.

Nearly seven weeks after the initial treatment, they introduced another round of DMG cells into mice that had already received B-SYNC.

Every treated mouse rejected the new cancer cells, demonstrating that the therapy's protective effects continued well beyond the initial elimination of the tumors.

Further observations showed that B-SYNC cells remained functional more than 70 days after treatment.

One possible explanation involves a problem known as T cell exhaustion. When immune cells remain activated for extended periods, they can gradually lose their ability to attack cancer effectively. By preventing CAR activation until the cells reach the brain, B-SYNC may help preserve their strength for when they encounter tumor cells.

The researchers believe this could be an important reason why their approach performed better than conventional CAR-T therapies.

"We didn't expect B-SYNC CAR-T cells to necessarily persist," Lakshmanachetty said. "But they are still patrolling for cancer over 70 days out -- and they're still very functional."

With the laboratory results demonstrating both tumor elimination and lasting immune activity, the UCSF team is now working to move B-SYNC into human testing.

Okada, Lim, and Lakshmanachetty are collaborating with UCSF cancer specialists to prepare clinical trials. The proposed treatment will use each patient's own T cells, which will be genetically modified to become B-SYNC CAR-T cells.

The transition from laboratory research to clinical testing is moving relatively quickly, reflecting the encouraging findings from the animal experiments.

The first trial will be led by UCSF physicians Marie Jaeger-Krause, MD, and Sabine Mueller, MD, PhD. Researchers plan to evaluate different combinations of intravenous delivery and direct administration into the brain.

For patients receiving ICV treatment, surgeons will implant a shunt connecting the brain's ventricles to a reservoir positioned beneath the scalp. This system will allow doctors to administer repeated doses of the engineered immune cells without requiring a new surgical procedure each time.

Although the treatment has not yet been tested for effectiveness in humans, its ability to completely eliminate tumors and prevent their return in mice has generated considerable optimism.

"Diffuse midline glioma is a heartbreaking diagnosis for patients and their families," said Mueller, director of the UCSF Pediatric Brain Tumor Center, UCSF professor of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Pediatrics, and co-founder of the Pediatric Neuro-Oncology Consortium (PNOC). "This preclinical data is very promising. Mice with DMG are being cured, and we are incredibly excited to bring this therapy to the children and young adults we care for. This is exactly the kind of innovative approach they deserve."
